subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMMUTATION OF DEATH SENTENCES
AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMMUTATION OF DEATH SENTENCES
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-115, to amend the Criminal Code (Commutation of penalty by provincial authorities).

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMMUTATION OF DEATH SENTENCES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMMUTATION OF DEATH SENTENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to transfer commutation of the death penalty to provincial jurisdiction.
I strongly recommend that the federal government forgo the prerogative it holds of commuting life sentences, as section 92, subsection 14, of the constitution gives the provinces the authority to administer justice.
In view of the tremendous new outbreak of criminality, I strongly support the Minister of Justice of the province of Quebec, Mr. Claude Wagner, when he advocates the upholding of the death penalty.

February 7, 1966
Questions
The federal government is constantly reluctant in applying the provisions of the criminal code, so much so that it has commuted all death sentences, even that of Leopold Dion, and this was rather shocking. The federal government could be relieved of this responsibility at the hands of provincial authorities who deem that the law should be strictly enforced in this regard.
My bill would simply allow the provinces to exercise their authority in that connection.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMMUTATION OF DEATH SENTENCES
speechtext:
Order, order.
Motion agreed and bill read the first time.

Background information regarding Question No. 197:
The special services division of the National Employment Service, is responsible for providing employment counselling and selective placement of special groups of workers. Competent physically handicapped persons, young people entering the labour market for the first time, older workers, veterans and long term ex-servicemen, those re-entering the labour market, workers wishing to undertake vocational training courses, and other similar categories of applicants receive employment services from special service officers.
Included among these categories of workers are those applicants identified as "personal problem" cases, the ex-inmate constitutes the majority of these cases. The ex-inmate is not statistically classified per se in National Employment Service reports. In each of the calendar year periods, 1963, 1964 and 1965, the number of personal problem cases placed was 6,826, 7,770 and 8,998 respectively.
The National Employment Service for many years has provided a continuing employment service to ex-inmates, including a visiting program to penal institutions. Special services officers regularly visit prisons for the purpose of interviewing, counselling and registering about to be released inmates. Documents concerning employment capacities of each individual are forwarded to the National Employment Office in which the ex-inmate plans to reside. A file is set up in the office so designated and efforts are begun to locate employment prior to the arrival of the ex-inmate. In some cases employment opportunities await the arrival of the ex-prisoner, this is especially true in the case of a skilled worker. Employers quickly discount the significance of a prison record of a man who possesses a high degree of skill. In the case of the ex-prisoner lacking easily marketed skills, his placement is of course more difficult.

1.	Was there a program of experiments sponsored by the government from 1959 to 1964 on rainmaking by means of the seeding of clouds?
2.	If so, what were the results of this program?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. Byrne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: DEVELOPMENT BOARD GRANT TO NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
1. Yes. From 1959 to 1963 cloud seeding experiments were sponsored by the government.
2. The results of the experiments suggested that small changes, either positive or negative, may result from this type of cloud seeding but that the chances of making large changes in rainfall by this method appear very slight. As expressed by the statisticians, the probability of an increase or decrease in rainfall greater than 22 percent was found to be less than 1 in 20. Because of the large natural variability of rainfall it was found to be impossible to be more precise about the effects of the seeding. These results are similar to those found in most other controlled tests of cloud seeding such as have been carried out in Australia and the United States.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of dicussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the explosive situation building up in the city of Oshawa concerning the strike between a local of the Toronto Newspaper Guild and the Oshawa Times, a situation which demands that this parliament discuss the archaic provisions of the Criminal Code with respect to picketing and take positive steps to modernize such provisions so that violence or other breaches of the law need not occur.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may be allowed to address myself to the only relevant question in this regard, the matter of urgency. This is a requirement of which I am well aware, having used this standing order before.
I would not have moved this motion today except that I and many others consider the situation in Oshawa to be a tinderbox which might well ignite if we in parliament do not act.
As Your Honour is well aware, the Criminal Code deals with the matter of picketing and, as a result of interpretations by the courts, picketing has been limited to three or four, or a small number of pickets. Such a view is out of touch with modern times, since

Mr. Justice Rand in his judgment said that picketing must have an element of moral persuasion which stops short of violence or force.
The very grave situation that has arisen in Oshawa has arisen because organized labour has tried unsuccessfully to convince various governments to amend this decision, and is now determined to obtain a review of this law.

The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) contends that Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 100, paragraph 1, puts this motion out of court because of the requirement that such a matter must involve the administrative responsibility of the government.
I draw the attention of the hon. member and Your Honour to the fact that this question has been under discussion a number of times and that on October 23, 1964, Mr. Speaker Macnaughton ruled that anything that comes under the responsibility of parliament may properly, other things not being against it, be dealt with under standing order 26.
The heart of my colleague's motion is that we should discuss something that is in the Criminal Code. I submit that the Criminal Code is the responsibility of parliament and that therefore as a subject matter it would be properly before us.
The other point that has been raised is as to whether there is urgency of debate; in other words, should we discuss it now or do we wait to be seized of this matter on the ground that there will be an appropriate opportunity to discuss it within a reasonable period of time?
It is our feeling that the seriousness of this matter is such that it should not wait until later in the day when it would be discussed off and on with other matters which could be raised under interim supply, but rather that

the House of Commons should consider this issue by itself at the earliest possible moment, which is right now.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)

What matters is whether the public interest might suffer if there is not discussion and debate in parliament. We think the provisions of the Criminal Code are such that a serious situation might develop in Oshawa within a matter of hours, and we feel this situation is one that this parliament ought to be discussing, by itself, at the earliest possible moment. I want to refer to citation 100, paragraph 1, where it is stated that the matter must involve the administrative responsibility of the government. This is a motion to adjourn the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the explosive situation building up in the city of Oshawa concerning the strike between a local of the Toronto Newspaper Guild and the Oshawa Times. The strike question is a matter coming under the administrative responsibility of the province of Ontario, not the federal government. Since this is the case, there is no way of bringing the subject matter of this strike under the jurisdiction of this parliament.
It is true that in the latter part of the motion the mover makes reference to the fact this parliament should discuss the archaic provisions of the Criminal Code with respect to picketing, and that steps should be taken to modernize such provisions. In other words we are asked to deal with an amendment to legislation. So long as the law remains as it is, and the matter is before the courts as I understood the hon. member to indicate it was, then that part of the motion, if it has any validity at all, would indicate that we ought not to be discussing the matter here at this time. Parliament has been very careful in such circumstances not to prejudice a matter before the courts.
On these two additional grounds I ask Your Honour to rule that the motion is out of order and not tenable here.

subsubtopic: OSHAWA NEWSPAPER STRIKE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
This is a most unusual motion. The argument in support of urgency is that tomorrow the question will be before the
February 7, 1966	COMMONS
court, and the expectation, based on the present state of the law, is that a decision unfavourable to a certain action anticipated or now being engaged in will be the result. This is asking parliament to do something it has no power to do. It is to that part that I take strong objection.
The motion refers to the archaic provisions of the Criminal Code with respect to picketing. It is not for me to say whether or not they are archaic. Then the motion goes on to say that we should take positive steps to modernize such provisions so that violence or other breaches of the law need not occur. The motion, sir, is a specious one and is worded in such a way as to cover the entire field. There must have been a recognition by the hon. gentleman who advanced it that parliament has no such authority.
What are we supposed to do? Are we supposed to talk about this on the basis of being afraid of what the judgment may be tomorrow. Is parliament, under the threat of fear as to the judgment, to legislate today on the subject of picketing? Parliament does not have such authority. This subject can be discussed at length when the motion for interim supply comes before the house. This motion is one that would be detrimental to all the principles of parliament, because whenever there is a fear that the law, as it now is, is going to be carried out then this parliament as a result of that fear is supposed to change the law. Surely the very expression of that proposition supplies the answer.
I am not entering into an argument about the dangers or possibilities of a serious situation. The proposition that parliament should act today in the belief that a law is out of date, and should change that law because the courts may render a decision tomorrow, is something I would not have expected to be advanced in this house.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I might say a word in explanation of the resolution now before the committee.

The funds requested in this resolution and the bill to follow are to cover government expenditures for the month of February in so far as can be done in this manner. In no instance is the total amount of an item being released and, indeed, where eleven twelfths of the items were previously released, no amount is asked for in this particular supply motion and bill. As hon. members know, all departments were presented in the supply motion of last week and detailed consideration is presently progressing in committee of supply. It is the government's intention to continue this consideration of government departmental estimates as soon as interim supply is granted.
The form of this motion and the bill to follow are the usual ones for interim supply bills. The passing of this motion and the bill will not prejudice the rights and privileges of members to criticize or discuss any item in the estimates when it comes up for consideration in committee of supply, and the usual undertaking is hereby given that such rights and privileges will be respected and will not be curtailed or restricted in any way as a result of the passing of this interim supply measure.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct my remarks to one particular aspect of this motion, the extent to which it deals with a request by the government in relation to Governor General's warrants. As I heard the motion being read by Your Honour, it seemed that the very last paragraph was in the terms which have been used in the past regarding a request for interim supply where in an intervening period Governor General's warrants have been used by the government in order to finance government expenditures.
It is my view that a practice has grown up which is invidious and wrong, and I think I would be derelict in my duties if I did not bring this matter to the attention of the committee and register my objection to it. I do call the attention of the committee to this practice and point out to the government that the time is long past when some remedy should be proposed.
I have obtained the orders in council in question and, as I roughly calculate the amounts, something over $900 million is involved. The expenditure of $900 million includes all the Governor General's warrants which are dealt with by this resolution. They have been paid under the authority of section
February 7, 1966

28 of the Financial Administration Act which provides in subsection 1:
Where an accident happens to any public work or building when Parliament is not in session and an expenditure for the repair or renewal thereof is urgently required, or where any other matter arises when Parliament is not in session in respect of which an expenditure not foreseen or provided for by Parliament is urgently required for the public good, the Governor in Council, upon the report of the Minister that there is no appropriation for the expenditure, and the report of the appropriate Minister that the expenditure is urgently required, may order a special warrant to be prepared to be signed by the Governor General authorizing the payment of the amount estimated to be required for such expenditure.
In my view the original intention of this section, an intention which has been completely lost sight of during many intervening years, is that only in cases where a payment is urgently required and not contemplated under ordinary provisions for government expenditure can the government invoke the provisions of this section.
The government will undoubtedly reply that other governments in the past have not viewed this section in that light. It is true that in the past there has grown up a very iniquitous practice in the use of this section resulting in the authorizing of expenditures to be made which should not have been made on the basis that they were not contemplated. I will read again the first two or three lines of the section which state:
Where an accident happens to any public work or building when Parliament is not in session and an expenditure for the repair or renewal thereof is urgently required, or where any other matter arises when Parliament is not in session in respect of which an expenditure not foreseen or provided for by Parliament is urgently required for the public good-
Surely there can only be one interpretation placed on that section, namely, that where some payment has to be made which was not contemplated and becomes necessary as the result of an emergency arising during a period when parliament is not in session, the government may then invoke the provisions of this section.
Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, that has not been the case in the past and I think it is high time we challenged the view now taken and suggested that something be done in this regard. Merely because a bank robber has been successful in the past in getting away with his actions does not mean that when he is finally caught he can invoke any statutory limitations. It is wrong to permit the executive branch of government to spend almost a 23033-52^
Interim Supply
billion dollars on the basis of a slim and slender reading of section 28.
This practice has been the subject of comment by the Auditor General. In the Auditor General's report to the house in respect of the fiscal year ending March 31, 1963, this comment appears at page 17, and the Auditor General was dealing with the question of Governor General's warrants. The Auditor General quoted the same section I have read and then said:
It will be noted that the above subsection simply authorized a "payment" which is "urgently required for the public good" when there is no other appropriation pursuant to which the payment may be made. The subsection does not provide for any control over the entering into of commitments during a period for which Parliament has made no provision nor does it appear to contemplate provision of a continuing spending authority to the Executive for the financing of general government services during such a period. However, this appears to have been assumed by the Treasury Board Staff in carrying out the procedure followed in preparing the special warrants for February and March 1963.
This is in reference to expenditures under Governor General's warrants during the period which followed the general election of 1963.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I think this is very neatly put by the Auditor General, I think he, by inference at least, takes the same view of the effect of this section as I do. He goes on to comment on some particular items, which I will deal with later, that were included in the Governor General's warrants for that year.
The matter was discussed in the Public Accounts Committee whose terms of reference covered a discussion of the Auditor General's report. Dr. George Davidson and other witnesses appeared before the Public Accounts Committee and questions were asked with respect to this particular method of financing the expenditures of government. In this connection I asked a question of Mr. Davidson, as reported at page 311 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Public Accounts Committee for the years 1964-65. I am pleased to say parenthetically, Mr. Chairman, that the Library staff are now indexing these reports of committees, which is very useful for members of the house. My question to Dr. Davidson was:
Dr. Davidson, perhaps I may be allowed to ask a question. Would I be right in suggesting that section 28 (1) of the Financial Administration Act was passed in contemplation of a situation arising following prorogation or a dissolution, when the normal situation would prevail and estimates would have been passed making provision for future

February 7, 1966
Interim Supply
proper expenditures, and that having been done, before a new parliament appeared on the scene an additional force was required to be sent to Cyprus, for example, or if a flood occurred requiring emergency relief, such a situation would fall squarely within the wording "Urgently required ?or the public good"?
As a result of these discussions, the statements made by the Auditor General and the evidence which was heard, the Public Accounts Committee recommended very strongly that the whole question of the use of Governor General's warrants should be the subject of study and discussion and should not be left in the state in which it was as indicated by our examination at that time. That was in July of 1964. Here we are in 1966 and we are now asked not to appropriate probably, because I suppose the money might be taken to have been appropriated, but at least to confirm the expenditure of this very large amount of money, some of which at least, I suggest, on a proper, ordinary interpretation of this section, has been improperly and illegally spent.
The minister shakes his head. I recognize that in the past the custom has been different, but custom cannot change, practice cannot alter, what is the plain, ordinary meaning of words. I think it is about time, before we are faced with another situation of this kind, that this matter was clarified. We left this house in June of 1964 certainly confirmed by what was said by the Prime Minister and others in the impression that we would be coming back in the fall to complete our study of the estimates and, if necessary, to pass interim supply again. In this way the expenditures of the government would have been made in the normal way. Instead there was a hasty dissolution and we now find that under those circumstances the government, having been compelled to draw on Governor General's warrants not for emergencies but for the ordinary general expenditures of government, is coming back to the house and asking us to approve and confirm this practice. I think the house should give some recognition to this particular fact.
It may be that if the government decides some amendments should be made to the Financial Administration Act they will come back and ask parliament to amend the act to clarify the wording of section 28 and provide that under conditions of this kind, where there is a period elapsing between dissolution and parliament being called, Governor

General's warrants may be used for the normal, ordinary, general expenditures which government requires to make. Personally, Mr. Chairman, I would have great hesitation in supporting such an amendment. For far too long governments in recent years have been encroaching steadily upon the constitutional prerogative of the legislative branch to vote supply. This is the one weapon we have that permits us to exercise control over government. The British North America Act calls for parliament to be convened once in a year, ostensibly of course for the purpose of granting supply as the case may be, and when Governor General's warrants are used in this way it constitutes a travesty of this constitutional right which should rest in the legislative branch of government.
It may be, however, that I am not in a majority in this view and that parliament may see fit to grant to the government, by proper, apt words and the necessary changes to section 28, the right to deal with ordinary government services by Governor General's warrants. But even if that should be the case-and this is something to conjecture; it is something for the future-I go a step further and suggest that a careful examination of this $900 million in expenditures by Governor General's warrants would include many, many items which certainly could never be brought within the definition "urgently required for the public good". For example, Mr. Chairman, I notice two items calling for the purchase of pictures, I think, or works of art for the National Gallery. How those could by any stretch of the imagination be construed as being urgently required for the public good is more than I can conceive.
This, I submit, is not simply a fractious and mischievous approach to this matter; I think it is a very serious transgression by this government of the ordinary, sound practices of parliamentary government and control by the legislative branch over the executive. In my view the time has now come when the government should take note of this situation and should take the necessary steps to see that this sort of thing does not occur again.
Mr. Chairman, if it is urgent that the Minister of National Revenue reply now I would defer my remarks.
No, Mr. Chairman, it is not urgent.

I did not think it was; that usually is the case. I should like to raise one matter which certainly is of concern to all
February 7, 1966

members of parliament, and I think we are perhaps the only ones who can do anything about it. This matter, which is and has been of concern to the Canadian public for many months now, in fact, we might say for the last two and one half years, concerns an attempt to bring about some stability of parliament itself, and I mean stability in terms of staying in business and thus being in a position to conduct the business of Canada without upheavals or the prospect of another election facing us for some reasonable period of time.
As we know, in 1963 and again last year the Canadian electorate decided that this was the structure of parliament they desired to have, regardless of whether one may agree or disagree with it. They decided that we would have a parliamentary arrangement whereby there was a house of minorities or, in other words, no one party would have more than half the number of members in the house in its own ranks.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
They did not decide that consciously it was the accidental result of the election.

My friend from Winnipeg South Centre says it was an accidental result, that it did not result from the conscious action of the Canadian public. I have a little more respect for the decision of the Canadian public than he does. I think it was a conscious action on their part. As I said earlier, the hon. member may not like what happened but it did happen. It is a fact, we are in the same situation as we were following the 1962 election and as we were following the 1963 election. We are in a situation in which one party does not have more than half the members sitting on its side. Unlike the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, I am one of those who believe we should accept the decision of the Canadian public and try to make the house work.
It is better than the decision they made in 1958.

There is some doubt in my mind whether or not the decision in 1965 was better than the one in 1958. Nevertheless, there is a necessity for parliament to develop some means of remaining in business for a reasonable period of time in the future. There is an absolute necessity for this parliament to ensure that it stays in business in order to conduct the business of Canada.

Just vote for the government and you will do that.

Perhaps if we had less interruptions from the voluble member for Winnipeg South Centre we would get along a lot better.
Talk some sense, then.

We can never forget, of course, the delightful contributions he used to make when he sat on the other side and occupied various ministerial positions, all of them without foundation.
There is not only a responsibility that devolves upon this parliament and its members but there is a strong, overriding responsibility that rests squarely on the shoulders of the Prime Minister. He is the first minister, the government leader and the one who initiates action and guides government policy. As Prime Minister of this nation he has the responsibility beyond that of the rest of us or of the leaders of any of the other parties. He has the undeniable responsibility of making a few points clear to parliament. He should, I think, announce his desires and his intentions with regard to the stability of parliament in terms of the length of time it should stay in business.
I believe he has a responsibility as well to announce some concrete steps to attain this particular end. If the government is defeated on a so-called want of confidence amendment, be it to a supply motion or the Speech from the Throne, whether or not it is classified as a want of confidence motion presumably a number of things could happen. One thing that stands out in our mind as an alternative is for the Prime Minister to proceed to the Governor General and indicate he is unable to continue, that he has lost the confidence of the house and recommends dissolution. This, of course, would be an unthinkable course to follow at this particular time in our history. It is one of the choices facing the Prime Minister in the event that one of these want of confidence motions carries or in the event that a piece of legislation is defeated in the house.
Another alternative, which I am sure my friends in the Conservative party will applaud vociferously, is for the Prime Minister to tender his resignation and select someone else from within the Liberal party to try to form a cabinet and another government. Another alternative, and this is perhaps stretching the possibilities under our constitution to the limit, is for the leader of some other party, presumably the next largest group in the house, to form a government.

February 7, 1966
Interim, Supply
Another alternative is that proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre during the Throne Speech debate, and it is one which was lucidly explained and well documented. It was the course of the government turning a blind eye to any such motion or amendment which was carried and continuing in office. I think we can see that all of these alternatives, some of which stretch the constitutional possibilities to the extreme in the event a want of confidence motion is carried, are not really satisfactory in terms of the stability of parliament. We have to keep searching for some other way.
I suggest that one of the things which must be done is for the Prime Minister to take the proposals advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and give them very favourable consideration. Before any amendments or motions of the type referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre were put to a vote the Prime Minister could announce that, regardless of the words in which they were couched, they would not be treated as want of confidence motions because of the necessity of maintaining parliament in operation to conduct the business of Canada.
Would the hon. member answer a question at this point?
I would be glad to listen to one.

All right. If the hon. member's suggestion is accepted by the Prime Minister, would that not put the party which the hon. member represents in control? The Prime Minister would have to accept their decision with regard to motions and the government would no longer be putting its legislative items before this house. The government would be put in a strait-jacket.
I think not, although I would say at the outset that if the party to which I belong had a greater say in the affairs of this nation we would be on a lot more stable basis than we are at the moment.
Obviously that is the biggest delusion since the beginning of time.

I heard a comment from an ex-Speaker, one that was obviously out of order. I would have thought he would know better than that after the years of experience he had in the chair. The suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would simply put the government in a position to conduct the business of the country as

they had set out to do. It would not put anybody in a strait-jacket, although it is interesting to note the reference to a strait-jacket and the source of the reference.
Another thing which might well be done, I think, would be to follow the suggestion made last year and reiterated again this session with regard to the proposal relating to capital punishment. Presumably this legislation will be dealt with on the basis of a free vote. In other words, regardless of whether the bill is passed or defeated parliament will stay in business.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I submit that with respect to most items of legislation except, perhaps, those of a financial nature arising out of the budget, it would be a simple declaration for the Prime Minister to make to say that such legislation would not be looked upon as involving want of confidence amendments and that the government was not staking its life on it but was asking parliament to treat it on its merits. If it was bad legislation and was rejected, the government would not also thereby be defeated. There would merely be a re-assessment of the situation and perhaps legislation might be brought in more nearly fitting the needs of the situation and meeting the feelings of the majority of members of parliament.
The hon. member for Timiskaming has what I think is a rather clearly developed and well thought out bill on the order paper, Bill No. C-57, which seeks to put a floor under the years of operation of a parliament just as there is now a ceiling. At the present time there is a maximum of five years between one election and another. The hon. member for Timiskaming merely seeks to establish a minimum period between elections of not less than four years unless by a two thirds vote the house expresses its desire to dissolve parliament before then and have an election. This is a commendable piece of legislation which the Prime Minister would do well to look at and, for the purposes of this parliament at least, it might very well be made statute law in order to guarantee some permanency and stability, within reasonable bounds, respecting the term of years of the present parliament.
I can foresee in this parliament, as was the case during the last parliament, that every time there is a throne speech, if we have more than one, or every time there is a budget presented or a supply motion introduced, there will be a guessing game whether
February 7, 1966

or not an amendment will be moved and will carry. The newspapers on each occasion, as they have on two occasions this session, will be exploring the possibilities of a defeat and Canada will be in a continual state of flux in relation to election campaigns. The country will be in a continual state of turmoil, anticipation and expectation that something which the people do not want to happen will happen.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that we must not try to play this game as we would the game of Russian roulette. We must not look to each succeeding vote in the hope that the hammer will fall on an empty chamber and that an amendment will not carry. I submit that one of the responsibilities involved in reaching the point where parliament can get down to the business of Canada with some reasonable assurance that it will stay here for some length of time is for the Prime Minister to take his position and functions as Prime Minister seriously. He should make some public announcement about the desires I have suggested and he should start off with a meeting of party leaders to see whether or not some continuity for this parliament can be worked out amicably. If it can be worked out-I do not know whether or not it can-and if Canada and this parliament can look forward to the next three and a half years with some guarantee that there will not be an election within that period, then this will be all the better for Canada.

It is identified as the centennial commission-1867-1967; there are no mistakes in the figures. But it is certainly not a draft. It is an official circular sent on behalf of the Centennial Commission.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that the centennial commission and the various departments should in the future be careful in matters of this nature, particularly so when it is intended for university students because university students are in a position to pick out these mistakes which are irritating, because they are making a real effort to improve more and more the beautiful French language we speak in Quebec and in other provinces of Canada.
Another point I wish to raise, Mr. Chairman, is the problem we have noticed for some time and which has existed for many years; I refer to the fact that on occasion there too often arises a conflict between Canadian citizens from various regions. Since the start of the session, this has been noteworthy as we could see in the last few days in connection with two different matters:
First, the rivalry between the ports of Montreal and Halifax. At Halifax, the citizens of that province or the members for those ridings seek to prevent the government from permitting icebreaker activity in the St. Lawrence river to allow winter navigation to the port of Montreal.
That is the point of view of the people of Nova Scotia and of the port of Halifax.
On the other hand, Montreal citizens would like to see the St. Lawrence open all year round so that traffic could go up to the harbour of Montreal and the latter could benefit from it twelve months a year. That is a kind of rivalry which should not exist because a town will never be able to maintain itself and grow at the continual expense of another town or region.
The city of Halifax or the Maritime provinces will not always be able to keep the work that is done in the harbour of Halifax by preventing it from being done in the port of Montreal. That can last some time, but not too long.
That is why no such rivalry should exist. If there is a need for winter navigation right up to Montreal harbour, if this is a question of progress, in accordance with modern times, something good for the country as a whole, then, it should be done. Such things should be allowed to come true. But the development of Montreal harbour should not be prevented

February 7, 1966
Interim Supply
merely because citizens of Halifax are opposed to it. You will not promote one city by trying to downgrade another, but by enabling each and every city to develop. The thing is to find for each city the suitable forms of development, those best suited to further their economic growth.
Mr. Chairman, this rivalry between areas always surprises me when, in Canada, it is possible for all areas, all ports, all cities to develop. I am convinced the port of Montreal has the right to develop as much as all the other ports, and in as much as winter navigation is now possible and practicable, the port of Montreal should benefit from the services of icebreakers.
Just think of it: in January, a Russian icebreaker or boat had to be brought in to free from the ice floes another Russian ship which lay trapped in St. Lawrence, while Canadian icebreakers could have done the job easily. But this has not been done, for fear of displeasing citizens from another area.
Another example is the number of questions asked today and a few days ago with regard to the repairs to the aircraft carrier Bonaventure. Of course, there are many ports and many shipyards in Canada needing work and which would like to get contracts. You have the shipyards of St. John and those of Lauzon. Tenders were called. The Lauzon shipyards across the river from Quebec submitted the lowest tender and are on the verge of getting this contract. But under the pretence that there is unemployment in another area, efforts are made to take away the contract from the Lauzon area and give it to another region in another province.
Well, everyone should know that there is just as much unemployment in Levis county, or in the surrounding counties, such as Dorchester, Bellechasse, Beauce or Lot-biniere. Unemployment is just as severe in these areas as in the Maritime provinces, but the government has used a most illogical method: tenders have been called but the government does not want to accept the lowest. The contract is meant for another area, just because there is unemployment in the Maritimes. But, Mr. Chairman, let us consider that there is just as much unemployment in the Quebec area and that it should be checked just like in the Maritimes.
Again, I say we shall never solve the problems of one area by trying to accumulate all the problems in another one.

The maintenance of unemployment in the Quebec area is not going to solve the unemployment problem that may exist in the Maritime provinces. Such a rivalry between those two areas should not exist. Every area should be allowed to develop and share in the economic development of this country. If the lowest tender was submitted at that time by the Lauzon shipyards, it is only normal that the contract should be awarded to them, and such a contract should not be taken away from them and given to another area merely because a few members of the house would like to see it awarded to another province.
Mr. Chairman, if every member exerts undue pressure to have contracts awarded in his area, this will entail competition between the various regions, cities and provinces. It is preferable to carry on with the established practice whereby the government asks for tenders, obtains information on the various contractors capable of carrying out the work involved and awards the contract to the lowest bidder, to the one most likely to do a good job. Then, this kind of competition will disappear and everyone will have an opportunity to tender and offer his services.
Mr. Chairman, we have witnessed this competition between various regions since the beginning of this session. In my opinion, this should stop, more especially with regard to Montreal harbour which some people would prevent from operating in the winter months by asking the federal government to refrain from using Canadian icebreakers to open the seaway up to Montreal harbour, under the pretext of helping the port of Halifax.
Well, Mr. Chairman, such competition should be stopped in my opinion. Each area, each province and each municipality should be free to make every possible effort in order to promote its own development.
This is not an appeal to partisanship, this is not an attempt to prevent another from developing; on the contrary, it is an appeal aimed at enabling every area and every province to develop.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak briefly on this interim supply motion. I wish in particular to protest the erosion of parliamentary rights as they relate to these interim supply motions. I hope the committee will not discount the sincerity of my contention because of the brevity of my speech supporting it. I do not propose to repeat the varied and substantial arguments advanced in this
February 7, 19S6



regard by the hon. member for Peace River with regard to Governor General's warrants and so on. I believe that granting supply and studying the estimates in detail was at one time and should be in the future the paramount prerogative of this elected House of Commons.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
This has not been the case during the past four years. For example, some of the departments have not had a detailed examination by the house for four years. You may recall that none of the estimates for 1962-63 were passed. The moneys were appropriated by Governor General's warrants because of the election campaign which took place between the first part of February and the end of that fiscal year. All that we had was some kind of subsequent supply motion but by that time all the money had been spent.
With respect to the estimates for 1963-64, six or eight departments were rushed through during the last two or three days. In fact, I believe four departments went through on a Saturday, the last day of the session prior to the Christmas adjournment, including one or two departmental estimates that members had been asking to have discussed for weeks prior thereto. I am not suggesting to the minister that we are in a position to do anything other than pass this interim supply motion and grant the remaining one twelfth some time before the middle of March, but I am rising to protest this practice and the way it is eroding the rights and paramount privileges of elected members.
When asked questions on orders of the day one of the favourite responses of ministers is, "Well, I cannot give you a detailed answer now but when the estimates of my department are under consideration we can discuss this matter in greater detail." We have had this kind of response and this postponement of detailed answers from year to year for the past four years.
We in this party think it is time we had a parliamentary discussion on transport policy with respect to grain and passenger service. The situation has reached the point where it is critical. Yet how long has it been since we had an opportunity to discuss railway policy thoroughly and how the railways are meeting the increased demand for transport? If you look at the records you will find it has been a very long time. That is only one subject and there are many others in the same category.
Today the Minister of Transport said he was praying that his estimates would be
Interim Supply
reached this afternoon and therefore I am not going to speak at length now. But if we are not to be given such an opportunity the matter is sufficiently critical that we should take time on this motion to discuss it. We should also have the opportunity to discuss the government's war on poverty, for it seems to be working in reverse with respect to some poverty stricken areas in Alberta which are in their present state through no fault of their own.
I note that the parliamentary secretary is going out behind the curtain but I hope he and his minister will use their influence, which I am sure is considerable, to arrange the business of the house so that members will have restored effectively to them what I consider to be their greatest prerogative, control of the public purse strings and an opportunity to peruse the estimates at least once a year.

Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member for Medicine Hat I, too, believe that brevity is of some consequence and I do not wish to talk at length. But I would like to take this opportunity while we are discussing interim supply to bring to the attention of the government some of the problems facing agriculture. I do not do this out of force of habit. I do it because of the visit which the Minister of Agriculture made to the western provinces a short time ago.
If we are to believe the press, the Minister of Agriculture acknowledged that there were serious difficulties in the farming industry and that there was a great need to find answers to the questions being asked by farmers, agricultural experts and economists. During his trip the minister was disturbed by the attitude of the Canadian Pacific Railway. He was shocked at the lack of box cars. He was unhappy about the inequality of quotas and he said something was going to be done. Let us hope the action taken is not too little or too late.
Because of the recent large wheat sales by western farmers there is an erroneous attitude in many other parts of the country that the farmers' problems have all been solved. Nothing could be farther from the truth. While grain sales have certainly helped to bolster the economy, they have also tended to conceal the unfavourable cost-price relationship which would worsen in the event of a crop failure or if Canada were unable to repeat these large sales and had to store large quantities of grain.

February 7, 1966
Interim Supply
One of the glaring inequities is inherent in the fact that farmers are receiving the same price for grain as they did 17 years ago. This statement was made recently by no less an eminent authority than Mr. Charles Gibbings, President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, when speaking at the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. It was also pointed out that while prices for grain had remained comparatively stationary during those years, the cost of production had increased by 54 per cent. Only by increased efficiency on the part of the farmers has the rising cost of production been absorbed, and the farmers have not been able to pass on the increased cost to the consumer.
Mr. Gibbings was not voicing only his own ideas. He was voicing the convictions of many farmers when he said that other countries had decided that the international wheat agreement price was insufficient and that those countries were subsidizing farmers to grow bread grain. In the six Common Market countries the wheat support price has been $3 per bushel and for Durum wheat $4 per bushel. Mr. Gibbings also said that the western farmers should not and could not be expected to continue to live on the price fixed under the international wheat agreement. We should give Mr. Gibbings some credit for coherent thinking and for making the policies of his organization known. He also made some suggestions which were embodied in a resolution that he presented to the meeting and which was adopted by it. Personally I have some reticence in believing in the efficacy of some of the suggestions he made but they certainly bear enumeration and discussion.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The suggestions embodied in his resolution included support prices for wheat, a guaranteed minimum wheat price based on production plus living costs, a forward pricing policy related to production costs on specified quantities of wheat, a subsidy on a basic quantity of wheat delivered in any one year, a two-price system for all cereal grains used for human consumption at home, and government payment of storage costs on all grain remaining in storage on July 31, the end of the crop year. No doubt some of these ideas are good but they are not a panacea which will cure the farmers' ills. The basic problem we must attack is that of making sure that the prices of wheat keep rising so that they will not be brought down by other countries' actions as has been the case in the past.

The Wheat Pool President is certainly well qualified to put forth ideas on agriculture and we welcome his suggestions. However, it seems passing strange that he should be the one in Canada to put forth ideas which should be accepted as policy by the government. Surely that is the duty and prerogative of the Minister of Agriculture. I can assure the minister that when he does put forth those policies which are in the best interests of the agricultural economy and the farmers at large he will receive the support of members in all parts of the house. We welcome the day and hope it comes quickly when some tangible evidence is forthcoming as to the government's intentions in the field of agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to participate in this debate on the suggestion of His Honour, the Speaker. You will remember that this afternoon I attempted, prior to the calling of orders of the day, to raise what I thought was a matter of great public urgency and importance. At that time Mr. Speaker, after listening to my argument in support of urgency, decided that the matter could not properly be heard at that time. I accepted his decision, of course. He suggested that the appropriate time to raise the matter again would be during the debate on interim supply. It is for that reason I wish to make a short contribution. Like other hon. members, we in this party are not anxious to hold up the interim supply bill but certain matters have arisen which are so vital to the welfare of Canadians that we feel they must be brought to the attention of the house.
When one moves a motion for the adjournment of the house it is always difficult to make an adequate case because of the restriction as to urgency. However, I do say that we did receive a reasonable judgment from all members of the house in this regard except the leader of the official opposition who took the view that this was a specious move on the part of our party. I am sorry he adopts the view that any attempt to deal with issues of public safety and welfare and a respect for law and order should be considered in the category of a specious move. What I want to place before this committee is a situation that is developing in the city of Oshawa and which in recent days has reached the point where it has now become explosive, almost a tinderbox which could ignite and create very serious trouble.
This situation arises out of a strike between a Toronto local of the Newspaper
February 7, 1966

Guild and the Oshawa Times which I believe is owned by Lord Thomson. The crisis has come about as a result of the application by the courts of the law under the Criminal Code as it applies to picketing. This strike is a legal and legitimate strike. The company applied for an injunction under the Judicature Act restricting the number of pickets. Organized labour for some years now has taken the position that the Criminal Code and its interpretation by the courts in so far as it relates to the law on picketing is very badly outdated and very badly in need of modernization. They are not alone in this view, Mr. Chairman. A great many other people experienced in the field of labour relations have delivered similar opinions.
The Minister of Justice announced the other day that the former Mr. Justice Rand has been appointed to a very important judicial inquiry. The same individual, the former Mr. Justice Rand, dealt with the question of legal picketing in an extremely important case known as Williams v. Aristocratic Restaurants reported in 1951, 3 Dominion Law Reports, at page 780. I do not propose to take up the time of the committee by reading the judgment of that eminent jurist but he did review the law and pointed out that in modern labour relations the whole concept of legal picketing has to be updated.
Under the Criminal Code, as most hon. members know, picketing is allowed for the purpose of enlightenment or the imparting of information. The courts have taken the view in their interpretations that this restricts picketing to a small number of people. In his judgment Mr. Justice Rand pointed out that the modern view of legal picketing goes far beyond that, that the right to picket means the right of moral persuasion, the right to have fairly large representation and the right to use every legitimate move to persuade the people involved in the industrial dispute as long as that persuasion stops short of violence. This is the modern view that for some years has been suggested should be incorporated into the Criminal Code.
The company involved in the labour dispute is to apply tomorrow for an injunction before the Ontario Supreme Court which is unprecedented in the history of labour relations. It is going to ask that all picketing be banned completely and that this basic right be removed from the people who are engaged in a legitimate and legal strike in the city of Oshawa. The labour movement has made it clear that it respects the principle of respect
Interim Supply
for law and order. No one has suggested that they do not hold the respect for law and order which is basic to a democratic system. However, that respect is a two-headed coin. One can only expect that people should respect the law when they feel that the law does not enshrine an injustice but that the law itself is just. It is only that appreciation which results in ultimate respect for the law of this land, and that is the point in issue in this case.
The labour movement has made it clear that it cannot permit a court order to be used to destroy a legal legitimate strike. We may disagree with them in this, and I am not taking issue with that, but statements have been made to the effect that if this course of action is pursued by the employer the collective trade union movement will be placed in a position of not being able to allow this to happen. This conjures up a vision of mass pickets. The mayor of Oshawa in a recent report has said that the local police could not possibly handle the situation, that the Ontario provincial police could not handle the situation, and that if the provincial police are sent there the army had better be sent too because that is what the situation will require.
It is for that reason we felt this afternoon that the situation in Oshawa has become so explosive and dangerous it was necessary for parliament to do something in an attempt to alleviate it. I suggested in my motion that one of the things we could do would be discuss the law of picketing under the Criminal Code and make it clear to the people in the trade union movement who are concerned that in our opinion this aspect of the Criminal Code is out of date and needs modernization and revision.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
If the parliament of Canada had been prepared to do that, I think there would be a lot less tension in the Oshawa strike situation tonight. However, in its judgment the house did not seem to think this was necessary. But let no one be under any illusions, Mr. Chairman. Far from holding people back from violence and breaches of the law, the present law on picketing in Canada encourages and creates situations which ignite this type of violent conduct.
What we should be trying to do is to modernize and bring this law up to date. It was suggested in the house this afternoon that by so doing we would be "caving in" to defiance of the law. Nothing would have been further from the truth. We would have been

indicating that the parliament of Canada is a responsible body of people aware of the explosive situation which has been created and welcoming the opportunity to express its concern and try to do something about it. Today was the day to have acted. I am sorry that we missed the boat. Mr. Chairman, I want to be very brief on this occasion. I note that the Minister of Agriculture is not in his seat. However, I hope that his officials will at least take note of some of the remarks I shall make and perhaps do something regarding a problem I have written to them about but with regard to which there apparently is not going to be very much action. Since the department apparently is not going to take any specific action, I feel I must raise this matter in the house on the first occasion available to me.
The problem about which I wish to speak briefly is perhaps related to one that exists in northern Alberta. It seems rather ironic that after a year when we have had such abundant crops in most parts of the west we should also have pockets of crop failure. I represent an area that happens to have suffered that fate. Strangely enough, perhaps half the constituency did not suffer as much as the other half. However, the point is that when farmers suffer a crop failure in the midst of plenty the pressure on those people to pay their accounts is as great or even greater because they are in direct competition with other farmers competing for seed grain and the like.
Whether or not the Minister of Agriculture realizes it, through most of the northern part of Saskatchewan, or at least that part with which I am familiar, we were not able to get our crops in at as early a date as usual because of heavy rains that lasted for perhaps three weeks. In the result much of the crop in this area was harvested very late. Because of the frost and rains that came our way the maturing of grain was delayed and as a result we were not able to harvest the crops until after we had had a snowfall. This snowfall resulted in much of the grain being unfit for seed for the present crop year and this necessitates the acquisition of proper seed.

I think the minister is relying to some extent on the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to deal with the problem in these areas and perhaps provide some of these farmers with needed cash. However, Mr. Chairman, the minister should take note of the fact that much of the area is not geared to an 8 bushel per acre crop from the point of view of surviving but to a 20 to 25 bushel an acre crop. This is the only way they can survive and if they get anything less they are in quite serious trouble.
I had occasion to write to the former minister of agriculture before that portfolio was taken over by the present minister. At that time I made several suggestions in this respect. I did not want at that time to burden the department with too many problems because I realized that the minister was giving up his portfolio. However, I did make several suggestions, one of which was that all payments made against farm improvement loans should be suspended and that no interest should be calculated during a year when there was a crop failure.
I hope the minister will see to it that no such interest is calculated in a year when there has been a crop failure because many of these farmers have had to buy very expensive machinery and find it very difficult to meet these payments. I think the Minister of Agriculture agrees with me that the price of machinery has soared to such a height that it is very difficult to purchase, and when the farmer finds himself in the position where he must purchase such machinery it is far more difficult for him to meet his payments. When you finish up in arrears you begin to wonder whether it is worth carrying on or whether you should give up the ship.
One other suggestion in my letter was that provision be made this year for sufficient seed grain to be available to these areas. I understand the attitude of the department is that these farmers can obtain a loan. But, Mr. Chairman, the minister should be aware of the fact that many of them have borrowed money to the hilt and cannot get further loans. It will therefore be necessary to make other provisions in order that a crop can be planted.
Another suggestion of mine was that there should be a moratorium on all accounts which may have accrued as a result of the year's operations. I appreciate that this may be difficult to administer and that in some areas it is not possible to do it. But I believe
February 7, 1966

the department should give earnest consideration to making some provision whereby additional loans may be obtained or the money made available in some other way. I know there are many areas in which credit has been obtained and the creditors would like their money back, and the department is in a better position to provide this type of assistance than the individual farmer.
Indeed, the department is in a better position to provide this type of assistance than are the banks. Some of the banks have been very reluctant, as a result of the government's tight money policy, to provide any loans. They say, "After all, we do not know how long this tight money policy is going to last. Furthermore, you are not even a good risk; you had a crop failure. What security do you have?" So the farmer finds himself in a position where he cannot obtain a loan with which to carry on his operation.
It seems to me that the department is relying too much on the prairie farm assistance program. I think the minister is by now aware of the fact that in order to qualify for prairie farm assistance farmers must form a block. There are many areas in which they cannot form a block because one happens to be in a particular corner or out of the way or in a strip, or some farmers along the way had a little better crop for one reason or another or perhaps had a smaller acreage and were able to get their crops in before the rains came, and so on. I do not want to elaborate on all the difficulties a farmer has to deal with, Mr. Chairman, but the point is that there are many areas in which a farmer does not qualify for this type of assistance.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Personally, Mr. Chairman, I am a firm believer in crop insurance. However, I do not believe the Department of Agriculture is doing enough in this respect. I had occasion to question the minister about this matter on January 20 and 21 when I asked a question supplementary to one already put by the hon. member for Peace River. The minister's attitude at that time was that because no requests had been made by the provincial minister he did not feel it necessary to take any action in this regard. I want to know who is at fault here. As I have said, Mr. Chairman, I wrote to the department in this regard. Certainly other people must have written to the minister because they wrote to me. If the minister of agriculture in Saskatchewan is at fault, I want that to be known. Furthermore, if the minister has communicated with the
Interim Supply
minister of agriculture in Saskatchewan, then I should like to know what steps the minister or his department is taking in order to help these farmers.
We hear so much these days about how many farmers are leaving the land. One sure way of making these farmers leave the land is by not providing assistance. I am sure if they were given assistance it would enable them to carry on through the next ten years. The situation is not a permanent one. I can recall that in 1959 the crop was snowed under and arrangements were made to provide assistance.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. I rather hesitate to mention the other problem I have in mind. However, I feel that the general attitude of the entire government has created a problem whereby the senior citizens of this country are penalized. I have communicated with the minister responsible for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation but I have not been satisfied with the type of reply his department has drafted. I do not know where I can turn except to bring this matter before the house.
An application was submitted by the Hudson Bay Pioneer Lodge to provide a senior citizens' home. I, along with other interested parties, the mayor and the contractor, approached the department to ascertain if this application could be accepted at their earliest convenience. On November 22 I was informed by Mr. Jean Lupin that everything was satisfactory. The department had inspected all the necessary documents and an order in council would follow. This was November 22. However, nothing was done. The contractor had submitted a very low bid in order to assist the project but the order in council was delayed for two and a half weeks. One has to remember that in the west the weather is cold.
The contractor did not know if he should proceed because in the meantime the cost of plywood was going up and the cost of copper was going up. Representations were made by the mayor, the contractor, the architect and other interested parties. I personally made

telephone calls to the minister and my secretary tried to communicate with his office. Nothing was done. In the meantime other applications were being approved. It was not until December that I was notified that approval had been given to this project. It seems to me that here is a clear case of the tight money policy of the government being applied to senior citizens, the wrong group to whom to apply it just as the farmers who suffered because of drought, frost or other hazards were wrong people to whom to apply it.
I wanted to bring these two matters before the house. I am sorry I took so much time that the minister found it necessary to ask if I would delay my remarks for a while. I felt the matters were of such importance that I should bring them up on this occasion.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I should like to make it clear that I was not attempting to make anyone listen to me; it is just that the hon. gentlemen who sit exactly opposite me were holding a conversation which was distracting me. I wanted all the time to hear what they were saying instead of concentrating on what I had to say myself.
I was saying that the Leader of the Opposition was mistaken when he suggested this afternoon that the motion was occasioned by a court motion to be made tomorrow. The fact is that an injunction has already been issued by the Supreme Court of Ontario. The injunction order was made by the court on Monday, January 31, on a notice of motion served, I believe, on the preceding Friday after permission had been obtained from the court to shorten the time for service. The injunction limited the number of pickets to four at one entrance and to three at each of two other entrances, making a total of ten. It is this limitation on the number of pickets which has caused the trouble now brewing in Oshawa and which has caused concern.
In my experience, Mr. Chairman, employers have used the law as found in subsection 2 of section 366 of the Criminal Code and the law of injunctions in order to attempt to break legal and peaceful strikes and have used it for no other purpose. I have seen in this case, Mr. Chairman, the affidavits in support of the first motion and have been informed of those in support of the one coming up tomorrow. There is not a suggestion in the original notice of motion asking for an order limiting the pickets, nor in the supporting affidavits that there had been any violence or other breach of the law.
As a matter of fact, since that order was made on January 31 the members of the union directly concerned, namely, the members of the Toronto Newspaper Guild, have never exceeded the number of pickets the order required. The pickets were swelled by the support and sympathy of a large number of other employees in Oshawa and its environs.
While it is true that the injunction is a matter of civil law and comes under provincial jurisdiction and that it flows from certain sections of the Ontario Judicature Act, it is also true that in making their decisions on injunction orders in relation to picketing the judges are guided by outmoded words in the Criminal Code. Section 366 of the Code prointerim Supply
hibits watching or besetting in various ways, and subsection 2 provides:
A person who attends at or near or approaches a dwelling house or place, for the purpose only of obtaining or communicating information, does not watch or beset within the meaning of this section.
It is sheer, utter nonsense to limit modern labour picketing to receiving or communicating information. This can be done much more effectively through the use of newpapers, radio or television. You do not need a person walking up and down in front of an entrance with a sign to communicate information, and information can be received, if there is any to be received, over the telephone.
Picketing by trade unionists-I will come in a moment to the question of a lawful strike-is for the purpose of winning support for their cause. I suggest that picketing is one of the important exercises of freedom of speech in our society. Picketing is an attempt by those who are on strike to persuade people not to go to work and to bring solidarity to their cause, to persuade customers and clients and other people dealing with the employer against whom the strike takes place not to make things easy for the employer by conducting business with him. All of that, Mr. Chairman, should be permitted by our Criminal Code if a strike is not to come bang-up against the law and against the issuance of injunction orders by the courts.
Some years ago a strike took place at any time the workers felt like striking and under the law it was lawful. They could strike in the middle of the term of an agreement or at any other time. Nowadays right across the country in all 11 jurisdictions of Canada -there are one or two provinces that do not have Labour Relations Acts-you cannot have a lawful strike unless you have gone through all the procedures which are provided for by the Labour Relations Act. The collective agreement must have expired. In the meantime you must negotiate, and if you cannot agree you must go through conciliation procedures. For this purpose there is a conciliation officer and a conciliation board, and only after the board has reported and some period has elapsed are you permitted lawfully to strike.
Thus, the law says to the employees of this country that a right which they had had for many years of withdrawing their labour when they felt dissatisfied or discontented they can no longer exercise lawfully except under certain conditions-after the passage of a certain period and after they have gone through certain procedures. When that has

Interim Supply
happened, as in this case-the Guild negotiated with the Oshawa Times for months and some two or three more months were consumed by the conciliation procedure-and still no agreement is possible, a lawful strike then takes place. Section 366 of the Criminal Code makes it possible for the employer to enter a courtroom and obtain an injunction designed and intended to hamper and frustrate such lawful strike. This is the reason trouble is brewing in Oshawa and why some of us-I make no secret about this-have a great deal of sympathy with those who are unhappy with the law as it now stands.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
It should also be recognized-this is another reason the hon. member for Danforth used the language he did in his earlier motion-that subsection 2 of section 366 which I read into the record dates from a provision contained in the Conspiracy and Protection of Property Act in the United Kingdom of 1875. This is why we call it archaic. Constantly in our law we pick bits out of some statute which was passed 50, 60 or 100 years ago and we leave it on our statute books unchanged. I am sure all hon. members will remember that the Criminal Code was completely revised in 1953-54, if I remember the year correctly; but even at that time, 10 of 11 years ago, we left that particular language the same or almost the same as it was in the statute of Great Britain dating back to 1875, a period when the trade unions were still fighting for the concept of legal recognition, let alone the legality of a strike and certain actions connected with it. These are the problems which now emerge and emerge as a result of the injunctions.
The facts of the legal battle are as I have stated; there has been no allegation even in the affidavits supporting the motions of any violence on the picket line. Unless I am mistaken, there is either an affidavit filed with the court at Osgoode Hall in Toronto today or mention of information in some affidavit to the effect that one of the officers of the police in Oshawa has confirmed that there has been no violence or threat of violence at any time on the picket line. Yet, Mr. Chairman, the number of pickets is limited and the union is threatened that an injunction prohibiting all picketing may or may not be granted tomorrow. The motion in court is that all picketing be prohibited and, more than that, that an order of mandamus issue to the chief of police of Oshawa, to the director of the Ontario Provincial Police, to

the sheriff and to all other sorts of officials to make people obey the earlier injunction or that which may issue tomorrow.
Every avenue of the court is used by Lord Thomson's newspaper in order to frustrate the lawful strike of some of his employees who in this case are journalists and white collar workers who feel aggrieved by the conditions under which they are being forced to work.
Furthermore, I also want to say that throughout the days of the strike not a single person who wanted to enter the plant has been prevented from doing so. Tenants, clients, customers and workers of this company have gone through the picket line if they have wanted to go through, undoubtedly to the displeasure of the picketers, a displeasure which may have been picturesquely expressed by some of them. None the less those persons I have mentioned were able to get through and did get through.
I respectfully submit, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Danforth is entirely right when he says that the house missed an opportunity earlier to deal with a matter which is of great urgency at the present time. Since we did not do it then, I am adding my voice to that of the hon. member in requesting and urging that the Minister of Justice look at section 366 of the Criminal Code and consider carefully the necessary amendments to subsection 2 so that the courts of the land may have a different direction as to how to deal with strikes. At the moment. I am not concerned with wildcat strikes or with unlawful strikes because they are in a different category. However, I suggest that employees who have gone through all the procedures of the law and who go out on a lawful strike should have the right to picket with any number of picketers they desire. So long as they picket lawfully they should have the right to persuade people to support their cause in any way they desire. So long as they picket peacefully they should have the right to impose whatever economic pressure they can impose on the employer. I emphasize that they should have that right so long as they picket peacefully.
The purpose of picketing and the purpose of the strike is to pit the economic strength of the organized employees against the economic strength of the employer. At the moment the law permits the court to throw an imbalance into that conflict betwen the striking employees and the employer. And when the law permits the court to come down on the side
February 7, 1966

of the employer against the employees by an injunction or by other procedure and thus interfere with the strike, at that moment the law is being used as a strikebreaking instrument, as it is now used, rather than as an instrument of meting out justice to people. It is this unjustice that is inherent in section 366 of the Criminal Code, and the fact that it can be and has been used as a strikebreaking weapon, that makes this issue so important.
