speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. A. Thomas (Middlesex West) moved:
subtopic: PRESCRIPTION DRUGS-SUGGESTED INCLUSION IN FUTURE MEDICARE PROGRAM
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider including the cost of prescription drugs in any national medicare program that may be established in the future.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion requests the government to take into consideration the inclusion of the cost of prescription drugs in any national medicare program which may be established in the future. It has been said that medical care is like a triangle. On one side there is hospitalization, on another side there are medical services while the third represents drugs. Inquiries show that at the present time no plans have been made to include prescription drugs in our proposed medicare program. I believe the Canadian public would welcome the inclusion of the cost of these drugs in such a program.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRESCRIPTION DRUGS-SUGGESTED INCLUSION IN FUTURE MEDICARE PROGRAM
speechtext: Order. I apologize for interrupting the hon. member but it is difficult for the Chair to hear what is being said.

subtopic: PRESCRIPTION DRUGS-SUGGESTED INCLUSION IN FUTURE MEDICARE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. If it is not practicable to include prescription drugs in our proposed medicare program then I believe the people of Canada are entitled to know the reason why. I hope the government can accept this resolution, at least to the extent of referring it to a committee for consideration. In any event the resolution should serve the purpose of bringing into the open some of the arguments both for and against the inclusion of the cost of prescription drugs in a medicare program.
I owe a personal debt of gratitude to several persons associated with the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada who have taken an interest in this question and who have supplied me with a number of pamphlets and reports relating to prepayment plans for the supply of drugs. As I say, I am grateful to these people. These reports indicate that practically all those concerned with this question recognize the

desirability of expanding the insurance principle so as to cover the cost of drugs. However, some authorities suggest that more research is necessary before further steps are taken.
Insurance to cover the cost of drugs is now available from a number of sources. These include Blue Cross, Prescription Services Incorporated, which is operated from Windsor, the public service group surgical-medical insurance plan under the major medical provisions of that plan, and various other plans where it is included as one item in major medical coverage along with special services such as ambulance services, private room services, and so on. Further, the government of Ontario, and, possibly the governments of other provinces, will, in cases where patients are able to qualify under a means test, pay the cost of drugs along with the cost of medical services.
Costs vary. Prescription Services Incorporated charges $1.90 per adult per month and 65 cents per child per month to a maximum of three children in any one family. These rates are for those covered by a group plan. For individuals outside group plans, where these can be accepted, the charge is 10 cents more per person per month in each case. The maximum charge for a family of two parents and three children insured under a group plan would work out at $5.75 per month. In the case of a family not insured as part of a group it would be $6.25 per month. There is an additional charge of 35 cents for each prescription filled. The maximum cost per family per year under Prescription Services Incorporated would amount to $69 under a group policy and $75 under a non-group policy. It is reported that the Alberta government has in mind a program covering prepayment of prescription drugs. Their estimated cost is a $25 premium per family per year plus $1 for each prescription filled. The Alberta government is also proposing to try out its plan on a selected group of people such as school teachers with everyone to be included, both young and old, so that the higher cost of carrying the risk for elderly people may be averaged out with the lower cost of carrying the risk for younger people.
In a study by the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada covering the cost of drugs in Canada, it is estimated that expenditure on drugs, whether bought from a pharmacy or dispensed in hospital, amounts to about $10 per person per year. This estimate is given in more detail on pages 352
February 7, 1966

and 353 of the report of the Royal Commission on Health Services.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
As many hon. members will be aware, the Hall commission on page 39 and again on page 349 of its report recommends that prescription drugs be included in a medicare program. On page 39, under item 5, prescription drug services, the report reads as follows:
In view of the high costs of many of the new life-saving, life-sustaining, pain-killing, and disease-preventing drugs, the commission has concluded that prescribed drugs should be introduced as a benefit of the health services program. Again, the decisions respecting the scope and priority of this benefit would be made by the provinces, but its authorization should be an early objective of the Canadian parliament.
Turning to page 349 of the report we find this statement, again repeating words used in the first part of the previous statement:
In view of the high costs of many of the new life saving, life-sustaining and disease-preventing drugs, of the unequal incidence of the burden of paying for these drugs, of the integrated character of health services, and of the fact that market forces do not operate effectively to regulate the drug industry, all of which subjects are dealt with in later sections of this report, the commission has concluded that prescribed drugs should be included as a benefit of any comprehensive health care program for Canada.
To leave non-prescribed drugs outside such a program, at first sight might appear to conflict with the point made above about the integrated character of health services. However, as has been stated already, competitive market forces are likely to regulate the production and sale of nonprescribed drugs.
In any event, there are apparently few if any non-prescribed drugs which are costly, for which there is a valid and appreciable need, and which may be properly used without medical supervision. Thus there should be little tendency for prescribed drugs to be substituted for non-prescribed drugs resulting in an unwarranted increase in social costs.
At page 345 of the Hall report they have this to say about the cost of drugs compared with the cost of medical care:
Expenditures on drugs place almost as heavy a burden on the average Canadian family as paying medical bills. In 1961, for example, expenditures on physicians' services amounted to $383 million as against $364 million spent on prescribed and nonprescribed drugs. In effect then, drug expenditures are equivalent to 95 per cent of expenditures on physician services.
If nearly half the cost of illness is involved in the procurement of drugs, then it seems to me that we should be just as anxious to include drugs under our proposed medicare scheme as we are to include physicians' services.

I now have some comments on the attitude of the drug trade and the attitude of the medical association to these proposals. I think it is conceded by all concerned that only with the wholehearted co-operation and good will of the drug trade and of the medical profession can any medicare scheme be fully successful.
Since our economy and habits of living are very much like those in the United States possibly some excerpts from a speech delivered by Dr. Montgomery, the President of the Illinois State Medical Society to the Central States Regional Conference of the American Public Welfare Association would be worth consideration. In it he said:
I know the standard complaint is that drugs cost the welfare department too much, that drug costs are getting out of hand, that they are "uncontrollable". On the other hand, I have checked some of the reports on vendor payments for medical care issued by the division of program statistics and analysis of the bureau of family services.
During 1963, vendor payments identified as for prescribed drugs made up 8.6 per cent of general and public assistance medical expenses, 9.3 per cent of public assistance medical costs. In 1962, the percentages were, respectively, 9.1 per cent and 10.0 per cent. And, just for comparison, in the fiscal year ending June 1958, "Drugs and Supplies" accounted for 13.9 per cent of general and public, and 14.1 per cent of public assistance medical care costs.
He gave these figures to show that drug costs, as a percentage of public assistance medical care costs, are coming down. Then he said:
If the parallel is not obvious, what I am trying to say is that the cost of prescriptions should not be considered simply as an added charge on the welfare budget, but in terms of what those drugs are saving the welfare department in terms of cost if they are not provided.
In other words, we cannot afford not to provide drugs because the cost will be greater if we do not provide drugs.
Dr. Montgomery summarizes it this way:
To my mind, this also leads to some question of the reality of drug costs as "a headache."
I might say that the speech was entitled, "Drugs: The Medical Care Program's Biggest Headache," and he goes on to show that he does not agree with that statement.
I wonder whether drug costs are truly so uncontrollable and such a matter of concern, or whether it is more that they are now becoming an identifiable and labelled medical cost, where before they were buried within the total cash grant.
In fact, putting together the statistical evidence that drug costs have decreased, as a percentage of total vendor payments in recent years and the fact that, during the same period, the number of states including drugs in their vendor payment

February 7, 1966
Prescription Drugs
programs has increased, perhaps our real question should be whether enough is being spent on drugs.
Then the doctor summarized the medical profession's chief objection to the inclusion of drugs in a medical care program:
The physician's real headache, as a physician, lies in his patient's not getting the drug the physician considers necessary tor proper treatment.
This is, I would say, at the root of almost all conflicts between welfare agencies and physicians in regard to agency control of drug expenditures. It is also at the root of any similar conflicts which might arise in regard to other phases of the welfare medical program, beyond those services the physician himself provides.
That seems to be the greatest beef of the medical profession, that governments in their efforts to cut down the cost of drugs try to impose control on the medical profession and the profession objects to this very much. This man puts it this way:
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
This gets down to the really basic controversy, where one exists, between physicians and welfare agencies on drug costs.
Later in his article he states:
Look at the matter like this-the Sears Roebuck catalogue lists phonographs for prices ranging from under fifteen dollars to over five hundred. They all have the same generic name-"phonograph"- and they can all play the same record, but you don't just order a "phonograph" and let the store decide which one to send you.
In other words, doctors want the privilege of recommending or prescribing drugs which they think best suit the patient and they resent any effort on the part of government agencies to restrict them in that freedom.
I do not intend to take any more time of the house except to say that the drug trade in general has accepted the proposition that drugs should be included in medicare programs throughout the North American continent. They could possibly oppose this inclusion and hold back the implementation of the programs for a year or two but they realize that they will eventually come and for that reason are generally prepared to accept that fact.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the motion proposed by the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) and to put myself on record on behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic party in support of the idea that

a national medicare plan should include hospital, medical and surgical services as well as prescriptions and apparatuses.
We agree with the view expressed in the Hall commission report that drugs impose a heavy burden on the public, particularly with regard to those people over 50 years of age and more especially in respect of old age pensioners. One has a heavy heart when he hears stories of some old age pensioners who pay more for drugs than they do for rent. The greater portion of their pensions in many cases is taken up by the high cost of drugs.
One of the reasons for the high cost of drugs has been the tremendous profits that pharmaceutical firms have made in the past. One would like to see some restriction with regard to the amount of profit they should make. There are two ways in which this could be effective.
First, there should be a working relationship between pharmacists and doctors whereby when prescriptions are given to the pharmacists they can fill them with drugs of a generic type rather than following the formula prescribed. The difference in the cost in this regard is very striking. The second thing that could be done, and will be done when a national medicare plan does come into effect and the government pays one half of the medical cost is to provide the provinces with an opportunity of incorporating into their plans the provision to which I have referred, thereby reducing drug costs.
Mr. Speaker, we are in full support of the motion put forward by the hon. member for Middlesex West.

subtopic: PRESCRIPTION DRUGS-SUGGESTED INCLUSION IN FUTURE MEDICARE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) on his presentation of this very "liberal" policy, if I may use that word. First of all, I should state that I agree in principle with the purport of his resolution. However, as he himself has said, we are dealing here with an expenditure of a great deal of money, almost $400 million, quoting the figures he used for the year 1961 as mentioned in the Hall commission report. When we speak about a medicare program for Canada we are talking about an expenditure in the neighbourhood of $1 billion per year, so you can quickly see that drugs represent a very substantial portion of the total cost, second only to the cost of medical services as provided by medical practitioners.
We are all aware of the different functions that drugs perform in curing illnesses and
February 7, 1966

preventing suffering and death. With the advent of newer, more potent and specific drugs we are finding that people who previously spent long periods in sickness are now able to go back to work much sooner. For this reason the Canadian economy is that much better. We have healthier people working for a longer time.
One of the interesting things that has happened with the advent of newer and better drugs is the decrease in hospitalization costs. As the hon. member mentioned, part of the cost of drugs is now paid for patients in hospitals who come under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. This cost is paid for under an agreement between the federal and provincial governments. The cost of hospitalization has been cut down because of the increased potency of drugs and their effectiveness. We are also finding that in respect of specific illnesses more hospital beds are available. The best example of this, of course, is in relation to the treatment of tuberculosis. Sanatoria which previously had long waiting lists now have empty beds. Many of them have been converted to hospitals for the chronically ill or elderly patients.
Another field in which I think the benefit of new drugs has been evidenced is the field of mental diseases. We now find that more beds are available not only because people have been cured but because more people are being treated as outpatients and do not have to be actually hospitalized as was previously necessary.
At this time I should like to put on record a portion of a statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) at the last federal-provincial conference in July of 1965 dealing with medicare. In respect of the proposal for medicare he said:
This proposal does not require detailed agreements governing the medicare plan. It calls only for a general federal-provincial understanding as to the nature of the health programs which will make a federal fiscal contribution appropriate. The federal government believes that there are four criteria on which such an understanding should be based.
First, the scope of benefits should be, broadly speaking, all the services provided by physicians, both general practitioners and specialists. A complete health plan would include dental treatment, prescribed drugs, and other important services, and there is nothing in the approach we propose to prevent these being included, from the start or later, if this were the general wish. We regard comprehensive physicians' services as the initial minimum.

speechtext:
In the statement that I read, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister did not say that. The Prime Minister said that the minimum under the first condition would be physicians' services and that a complete health plan would include other things such as prescribed drugs, but the benefits at first should be those services provided by a physician whether he be a general practitioner or specialist. Perhaps I will clarify that point later. Speaking at the same conference the Prime Minister said later:
Prepaid medical care is the largest item in a complete program for health services, but it is far from being the whole of such a program. There are other areas in which either joint action or the concerting of parallel federal and provincial action ought to be considered.
One such area which we referred to in the last Throne Speech was the quality and availability of drugs and their relation to the prices that the public has to pay. As you know, parliament has established a special committee to enquire into these matters. We hope that its recommendations will have the effect of reducing the prices of drugs, and thereby make it easier for a complete health service to make drugs prescribed for major illnesses available on a prepaid basis.
I am sure every hon. member is aware that the committee mentioned in the Throne Speech before the last one actally was set up in the last parliament with the specific terms of reference to make recommendations to the government on things that could be done to bring about a reduction in the cost of drugs. That committee met but unfortunately it only met once or twice. However, the groundwork of the committee is there. The people who were to appear before the committee had already been contacted and professed an eagerness and willingness to come to talk about the cost of drugs. I am sure they are more than willing to come forward in this session.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, in the last Throne Speech it was repeated that this committee

February 7, 1966
Prescription Drugs
should be set up. We are looking forward to it being set up and hope that it will be able to present a report to the house on this question.
There is no question that the cost of certain drugs in common usage is very expensive in terms of dollars and cents. There is also no question in anyone's mind, I am sure, that many of these drugs are worth this much and much more in terms of the benefits they can give and the lives they can save.
There are many ways of measuring cost. If one compares, for example, the cost of drugs in proportion to the standard of living, I understand that Canada has the second cheapest drugs in the world. I should like to mention a few of the things that do contribute to the cost of drugs because whether, as the hon. gentleman suggests, the government underwrites this cost in the form of a medical care program or it remains in the field of private enterprise, it is very important that the price of drugs be brought down.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, dealing with the basic or raw material from which a drug is made, it can be found either naturally occurring or is made chemically. Usually a drug that is found naturally is later made chemically in a much cheaper form. Often this basic material is imported into Canada, and is sometimes merely processed and packaged here. Because of mass production systems available in other countries, particularly the United States, it is often cheaper to import a drug than to make it in Canada. As an example, Mr. Speaker, I understand that there is no drug firm in Canada that manufactures penicillin; it is much cheaper to import it from the United States.
As this problem is related to the relatively small Canadian market in comparison with the United States, I really do not know the answer to it but would only say in passing that to place a higher tariff or tax on these imports into Canada would merely raise the price of the drug, which would have the opposite effect to the one for which we are searching. In dealing with drug research, Mr. Speaker, most of the companies quote a figure of approximately 8 per cent of their budget that is spent on drug research. Unfortunately in Canada at the manufacturers' level drug research is very limited. Most of the research is done at company headquarters and most of those companies with 100 per cent owned subsidiaries in Canada are now located in the United States, Switzerland or England.

Just a short while ago the only remaining large Canadian drug firm in this country passed into American hands. The drug companies point out that drug prices in Canada include the cost of research done elsewhere and justify this by saying that because Canadians benefit from the research done elsewhere we should share in that cost. A certain amount of research is done at the university level and financed by the federal government under the Medical Research Council. In passing I would say that the federal government is going to have to take more drastic action in this field and increase by a great deal the amount of money available for medical research in Canada.
So far as the drug manufacturer himself is concerned, he is usually but not always the one who discovers the drug. Some manufacturers, however, do no research at all. I shall come back to that point in dealing with price. Some manufacturers only manufacture a drug and market it. As a doctor I could manufacture drugs in my basement or my office if I wished to do so, and as long as I did not sell those drugs I would be conforming to the present laws under the Canadian food and drug directorate.
Drug manufacturers do research in many ways, all of which are expensive and all of which, because the market is competitive, they do independently of each other. They may test naturally occurring substances. For example, antibiotic manufacturers test thousands of samples of soil yearly from all over the world. Many antibiotics have been discovered this way. Manufacturers may take a drug with a known activity and try to change it in some way chemically either to make it act differently or to make it less dangerous to the human body. No drug, including aspirin, is completely safe to the human body. Any drug that is used carries with it a certain risk, and this is a fact that the medical profession has to take into account every time a drug is prescribed. One has to balance the risk involved in taking the drug with the risk involved in not taking it.
The researcher has to run a series of tests on new samples he has made on the chance that one out of many thousands may prove useful. Many manufacturers take well known drugs and combine them in various ways looking for a combination more effective or more aesthetically appealing than the product of their competitors. For instance, I am sure there are thousands of different kinds of stomach remedies on the market that literally
February 7, 1966

all contain the same type of drugs. I would hope this would be one area in which the price would be controlled and in which manufacturers would co-operate to cut down repetitive products on the market. Research in the medical field, as anywhere else, costs a great deal of money and most of it never produces a worth-while product. It follows that when a good product is discovered it unfortunately has to pay for all the research on all the products that were never of any value.
[DOT] (6.40 p.m.)
I should now like to say a few words, Mr. Speaker, about so-called generic drugs as against ethical drugs. Often cheap drugs are available that are made by what is referred to as a generic drug firm. That is a firm that sells drugs under the chemical name rather than a trade name. A generic firm generally produces a drug that has been developed by some other drug company. These companies do no basic research and no research on new effects of old drugs. They are literally manufacturers of products, in this case drugs. Because they do not do research they are able to sell their drugs cheaper than a company that does research. The medical profession often hesitates to prescribe the cheaper drugs because they are unsure of the Quality.
As I said before, there is nothing to stop people making drugs in their own garage provided these drugs have passed the food and drug directorate at some time. I have been told that in the near future the food and drug people in Ottawa will be licensing manufacturers and this will allow the directorate to know when and where every manufacturer is operating. The doctor wants to be sure not only that what he prescribes is actually the drug he has ordered but also that it will do the job that he intends it to do.
I should like to mention at this point that I do not want anyone to get a wrong impression. I am sure there are many generic firms in this country which undoubtedly do produce high quality drugs. As I am sure everyone is aware, the discoverers of medicines are protected by patent. The medicine itself it not patented but the manufacturing process by which it is produced is patented and protected for 17 years. There has been a great deal of controversy over medical patents. The restrictive trade practices commission recommends that they be abolished. However, the Hall commission recommended that they not be abolished for a period of five years but that freer use be made of the compulsory licence provision whereby a company applies
Prescription Drugs
to a court for permission to produce a certain patented drug and pays a royalty to the company holding the patent. If a new drug is not protected by patent, then any company can make the drug.
Naturally a firm can make a drug more cheaply if it does not engage in research. The major drug companies have stated that if they are not protected by patents, which literally give them a monopoly, they cannot afford to conduct research on new drugs and research will cease. They point out that countries without patent protection, such as Italy and France, have not made any major medical discoveries for many years.
In so far as drug promotion is concerned, once a drug company has developed a new product a market must be created for it. This is done in many ways. Most products of value medically are available by prescription only and therefore the company has to sell the doctor. This is done by advertising in medical journals as well as by detail men who call at the doctor's office. The distribution by mail of unsolicited samples has ceased, partly because of recent amendments to the Food and Drugs Act. Most of the mail that crosses a doctor's desk crosses it rapidly and ends up in the wastepaper basket. A great deal of money is spent on the promotion of drugs.
One of the suggestions made by many people, including the Hall commission, for controlling these promotional activities is a change in the income tax law to allow companies to deduct expenses for only a certain proportion of their promotion budget. The figure usually mentioned is 15 per cent.
In so far as the federal sales tax on drugs is concerned, Mr. Speaker, this is a tax imposed after the drug is manufactured and is paid directly by the company just as it is on any other product. Personally I am in favour of the removal of the 11 per cent sales tax on drugs provided the saving is passed on to the consumer and does not end up in someone else's pocket.
In dealing with the Hall commission report, Mr. Speaker, may I cite something Mr. Hall said at page 40 of Volume 1:
It is no accident that the public interest has increased in direct relationship to the efficacy of drug therapy and the high cost of many of the most effective drugs. Expenditures on all drugs are equivalent to 95 per cent of the outlay on physicians' services with prescribed drugs representing about 43 per cent of medical expenditures.
On the next page of the report I find this:
That in the provision of the drug benefit, there should be required a $1 contributory payment by

February 7, 1966
Prescription Drugs
the purchaser for each prescription, subject to such discount as the retailer may offer.
In passing I should like to say that I oppose that principle.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRESCRIPTION DRUGS-SUGGESTED INCLUSION IN FUTURE MEDICARE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to talk the bill out. I am going to leave that for another hon. gentleman. I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) on the very competent manner in which he discussed his notice of motion. I think that fundamentally he stuck to the real issue, that there is no valid excuse in this day and age for a single Canadian to be denied the benefits of medication. This is not the time nor the place to discuss in depth the cost of drugs because time does not permit.
I noticed that the hon. member for Middlesex West did not use those automatic phrases, "the high cost of drugs" or "the

exorbitant profits of the drug industry". As a member of the Food and Drugs Committee who has attended 28 or 30 sessions of that committee, I feel that these cliches are subject to question. What is more important, Mr. Speaker, is that we have a duty to all Canadians to make sure they are not denied medication. I think that the cost of anything, including drugs is a relative matter, and that the payment of 50 cents, 75 cents or a dollar for prescriptions in addition to the cost of medicine is a distinct hardship to thousands of Canadians who live on $75 per month.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
Certainly medication costs of $10, $15 or $20 are of no consequence to many people who can afford them and who spend such sums on many other items of a more luxurious nature. In a few weeks time or less I hope that the Food and Drugs Committee to which I referred will meet again under the chairmanship of the learned member who has just taken his seat so that it may enter the second phase of its investigations into the cost of drugs.
The Hall commission report made many suggestions as to how the cost of drugs can be controlled or reduced. As a member of the Food and Drugs Committee I took the trouble to search through the library and to look into the available statistics of the percentage figures for expenditures by the Canadian pharmaceutical industry on promotional material and on that phase of their operations more familiarly known as marketing.
After doing a little arithmetic and having my facts very well substantiated, Mr. Speaker, I was amazed to find that according to the annual statistical survey of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada for the year 1963, which was the last complete year I could get, 26.6 per cent of the sales dollar was spent on marketing. But the significant thing, Mr. Speaker, is that the amount spent on literature, the most obvious thing that comes repeatedly to mind, is one cent of the cost of a prescription, just one copper. This one cent goes directly to the production of promotional literature in this country. This amazed me, Mr. Speaker, and made me dig a little deeper. I found that the problem in this case is even further complicated by the fact that every pamphlet must be published, as it properly should in this bilingual nation, in both English and French. Those of you who may have some relationship with the graphic arts industry know what an extra financial burden this places on the pharmaceutical industry.
February 7, 1966

I could speak at length on this question but I know another hon. member would like to say a few words. However, one thing which has intrigued me in the debate this evening is the fact that we who feel so pro-Canadian-I know I feel this way-and at times antiAmerican in the industrial field are in a sense on the horns of a dilemma. If we are to encourage Canadian industry, we find ourselves in the unfavourable position of not being able to produce such life saving drugs as penicillin in this country without its production being heavily subsidized by the Canadian government. Therefore we are left with the unenviable choice of welcoming the importation of this type of drug into Canada to the detriment of the Canadian industry. I mention this because the firm of Frosst, which is close to my riding, has been purchased by United States interests.

subtopic: PRESCRIPTION DRUGS-SUGGESTED INCLUSION IN FUTURE MEDICARE PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is one particular reason why I accept the dubious honour that has been bestowed on me by my colleague from Verdun and it is that I have a particular interest in one aspect of the matter now before the house. I refer to the drug companies themselves. I noticed the reaction of some of the members in the New Democratic party when the hon. member for Verdun announced the honour that was to be mine. Perhaps those in that group will agree-I hope they will-with what I am going to say about the drug industry. Personally, I should like to think that we could nationalize the drug industry.

subtopic: PRESCRIPTION DRUGS-SUGGESTED INCLUSION IN FUTURE MEDICARE PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PRESCRIPTION DRUGS-SUGGESTED INCLUSION IN FUTURE MEDICARE PROGRAM
speechtext:
However, I realize this would be a difficult thing to do owing to the fact that so many United States companies are involved. Therefore, if we could bring the United States companies into line perhaps what we ought to do is to internationalize the drug industry in both countries.
I say this because it seems to me that those in this industry have a greater responsibility than those engaged in the manufacture of soap. I see no difference in the way the drug manufacturers conduct their business and the way those who manufacture soap conduct theirs. Perhaps the people of Canada would not mind paying a few extra cents for their soap if they knew that some of their money went into promotion and advertising which in turn would pay for "Bonanza" and other popular programs. But when a considerable amount of the consumers' money is used in this wasteful way by the drug industry I think it is a different kettle of fish.
23033-53J
Prescription Drugs
Accordingly, I feel that when this matter comes before the committee on food and drugs serious consideration should be given to the proposition I have put forth. I realize the difficulties involved and they do not arise just because the industry is not nationally owned or centred in Canada. I could go on at great length-I should like to do so at some later date-to list some of the particular aspects of waste and inefficiency in the drug industry which, in view of its importance to the general public of Canada, should come under much stricter control and regulation than is now the case. It seems to me that it would be desirable, if it was in fact feasible, to nationalize this industry.
I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that the general motion introduced by the hon. member is one I support wholeheartedly, though the one reservation I have about it is that if the industry is going to conduct its affairs as it is now it would be better if we paid for these drugs out of public funds than ask people who can ill afford to do so to pay for them themselves. It would be a far more desirable state of affairs if this could be avoided, but I do not think the matter of free prescription drugs can really be considered without taking into consideration some of the complaints which many Canadians have about the operation of the drug industry. In saying this I am in no way casting reflections on individuals who are necessarily engaged in the industry; I think it is the system that is at fault. They think they are in the same kind of business in many ways as soap manufacturers when in fact they are not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I did not interrupt the hon. member before the private members' hour but I am wondering if he has taken into account

the fact that some of the remarks he is making now have to do with a decision of the house which was passed by a resolution on January 21 regarding the new rules of the house. Has he taken that into account in the remarks he now makes?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. I realize that this is the vehicle that caused the difficulty. What I am really discussing is not the rules or the changes in the rules but the results of those changes, as they affect members of the staff, and also to the extent that we are involved through legislation for the payment of wages to that staff. I agree that the house has made certain changes, and I should not presume to refer to those changes except with respect to the end result which, as I see it, has arisen from this particular change.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I would respectfully submit to the Chair and to the hon. member that the remarks he is making with respect to the decision of the house, that private members' hour will be during the dinner hour, are out of order. However, I should be willing to undertake to the hon. member to take the matter of staff up with the commissioners of internal economy to make sure that the house is adequately staffed to carry out its decision, which was that it should sit through the ordinary dinner hour.
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate those remarks probably as well as the minister does. However I think that this was not really a point of order; it was an explanation.
A commitment.

Yes, also a commitment which I am doubtful can be honoured, although it has already been undertaken.
May I say something in regard to some observations I made earlier? I believe I mentioned the translators. I apologize to the house leader for having used that word, because what I really meant was the interpreters. The interpreters staff of this house has a complement, as established I believe by the internal economy commission of the house, of 17 members. I presume, and I am only presuming, that Canada does live up to the labour code, and to the code that the Interpreters International agrees to, that allows intepret-ers to work for certain periods and to have certain periods off. The Canadian government has violently abused this code in the past.
February 7, 1966

The reason the government has abused that code is that interpreters are very scarce. We cannot get a full complement. The 17 interpreters the house is supposed to have turn out to be only 12. I suggest that this is not a sufficient number to carry out the duties they are going to have to carry out. Anyone who has studied the matter will know that the rules which have been laid down by international agreement indicate that these persons are being abused in the work they have to undertake in committee, and that they therefore find themselves taxed beyond their capabilities. That would be so if they were called on to do translation work in the house without taking on the added onerous job of committee work. However, the government has also used these people for what I call outside committees, and they do not pay them for these. They are hired by the year. They are on salary, and therefore they are working buckshee. They are moonlighting on behalf of the government, on the orders of the government, and the government takes advantage of these people.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that all members of the Liberal party, who were so very proud of the terms adopted in the new labour code which they were willing to tell everyone about during the recent election, would agree that at least the same kinds of terms should be applied to the people working in the House of Commons. I spoke to a member of the staff during the private members' hour, and I find that the system used is a very odd one, because some members of the staff decide that they will go and eat, and they have not really any replacement at all. They just slip out whenever it is possible to, get something to eat, and come back. There is no replacement.
These conditions should not exist. I should like to think that I am not out of order, but may I ask why they exist? I should also like to say, confining my remarks within the rules, that there are a number of things that a private member can do about this. You may have noticed during the debates of this house that the Prime Minister is very seldom if ever here, and also that most of the cabinet ministers are not here. There is some kind of tacit agreement that things should not be left entirely alone, and there are usually two ministers here. That may vary. I have no objection to this. If you look at my party you will find that we have a tacit agreement that we are not here all the time.
I think it might be advantageous if we were here. I think it might be advantageous
Interim Supply
for the house to operate as a real committee, with most of the members in that committee. I suggest a number of things, Mr. Chairman. My first suggestion would be that we take a roll call. That does not mean that the Clerk Assistant of the House should rise and call everybody's name. However, I think that there are ways we could have a roll call. It is a fact that there are members who are never in this house from one month to another. I have not been here very long, but I have been here a few years. However, in my opinion there were more members in this house for the several votes in the last few weeks than I have ever seen before.
This may be a good thing. It may also produce some very interesting results in the next few weeks. Mr. Chairman, what I am getting at is that I think the house should function properly, and to enable it to function there should be some rules. The Prime Minister or house leader should be in the house occasionally, and they should be prepared now to tell us what the timetable for the rest of the session is. They should be able to tell us now if we are going to have an Easter recess, not for my convenience to enable me to know what I am going to do, but at least so that the staff who work for us in the house and in the complex surroundings it should know what they will be able to do, and how they are to arrange their business.
Mr. Chairman, if some things happen as I expect they will, in the next few weeks, we might pass through some items of legislation embarrassingly quickly. If that happens the government may have to call a recess that it is not prepared for.

This has happened
before?

Yes, it has happened before. I can see that this might be embarrassing. I do not think governments should operate in this way. I think that there should be a timetable, and if the government is going to have a summer recess, then why not say so now?
I am unhappy with the fact that parliament has a gun to its head all the time. If it is not the government, then it is the opposition. It is undoubtedly true that there is a gun held to somebody's head all the time to get something done to suit somebody, on some particular occasion.
This is an impossible situation. Soon committees will start at nine o'clock in the morning and go to 10.30 at night, theoretically without a break. That will not be impossible for members of parliament who, I know, are

February 7, 1966
Interim Supply
endowed with a very strong constitution, but at least let us think about the staff who are going to be involved in this stupid rat race we are setting for ourselves.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
I think the government has an obligation to act in these circumstances. The Prime Minister also has an obligation. I am sure he did not take into consideration the fact that people would be sitting through their lunch hour when he decided on a six months' recess last year. We were in an awful hurry before that election was called. It was doubtful whether we could get away by June; but we did get away all right. Then the Prime Minister decided that an election should be called. Time went by; the recess lasted six months. Now we have this terrific rush again. Let us look at the reasons for it. We have designed rules to take care of many of the problems which face us. We brought in one rule which would enable a start to be made on our committees work as soon as parliament met. But the committees have not been set up yet, though the business of the session is already almost a month old.
Mr. Chairman, the committees will be meeting, the house will be meeting and everything will be happening at the same time, all of this involving exactly the same people who function for the rest of the year. In any other establishment some kind of organization would be set up to deal with this chaotic situation. It is not your responsibility, Mr. Chairman, but you are well aware that we asked a senior civil servant to assist us in the better arrangement of our affairs. What happened to him? He ended up in the hospital and as soon as he got out he decided to quit. I don't blame him one little bit. He found that in all his experience there was no way of bringing organization into this chaos. Why do we not sit down for a few hours and try to reach a sensible solution. We are not going to make this country happy by arranging to work from 9 in the morning until 11 at night, if attendance is to be limited to the few members who are present in this chamber now.
Where are the rest? They went for supper; they are taking their turns. Well, Mr. Chairman, if parliament is of no value, why do we have it at all? If it is of value why do we not arrange to allow as many as possible to participate in its work. We should not sit through supper at the expense of the staff. This protest which I am making will probably not get anywhere. In all probability nothing will be done about it.
Headlines.

I missed that. I do not think anything will be done about it because the people who could do something about it do not want to do anything about it. We can make all the silly changes in the rules that we want to make, but we shall have to change them more fundamentally if they are to meet the needs of the time, with all the many operations which have to be carried out. We are now discussing estimates from last year. We are being asked in interim supply to pass estimates in relation to money which has almost been spent. We are reaching the stage when eleven twelfths will have been spent. It is important, they say, that we should pass these estimates quickly. If that is so, why did we take a six months' holiday?
We have reached a stage at which we have decided to make changes in our rules in order to help us carry on the nation's business-not that this will help members of parliament. I have belonged to a number of organizations. I have been associated with the labour movement for a long time. I have taken part in the work of many committees and seen a lot of work done, but I think there has never been a committee in which I have been involved which was less apt to get things done than a committee of the House of Commons.
I believe the rules of parliament could still be improved, and if hon. members wish to improve them I suggest they do so. But merely lengthening the hours will not accomplish their purpose. You were here, Mr. Chairman, when we facetiously said at the beginning of the session that we would add a couple of hours to each day. Do you remember when we extended the hours and the hon. member for Port Arthur, the late Mr.-
Oh, oh.

Our late colleague, our recent colleague, our departed colleague, made a motion extending the hours. But he forgot one thing. We had agreed that we should also sit on Sunday, because this was a day which seemed to be going to waste. He deleted the part about Sunday but left in the other extended hours. And the house went on to establish the longest session in parliamentary history up to that date. Instead of shortening the session we had lengthened it. Indeed, it could not possibly be any longer. It went on from one date to a year later at another date, and failed to accomplish anything at all.
Perhaps we are not competent to make the necessary changes. Perhaps we are not adult
February 7, 1966

enough in this place to do anything about it. But I would point out that we are now likely to be here for three or four years, if only because most members of parliament are well aware that nobody in the country wants another election. They are also aware that most members will find it necessary to accomplish a good deal of business if they are to be returned after the next election, whenever it takes place.
This should make for a good parliament. But we need to consider carefully what we are doing to the staff and to ourselves. We need to consider whether we can arrive at a better way of doing business. There is no need to fight another election. Hon. members need not throw campaign speeches around any longer. Ever since 1957 when I was first elected to this chamber every member has been campaigning constantly from the day he arrived till the day he had to leave. Perhaps this was understandable, since no one knew when an election might come. But I am sure that the Canadian public is not prepared for another election. This means that the people in power are probably not ready for one either. If we are to be here for another two or three years let us plan accordingly and do something sensible about the rules. Mr. Chairman, if we do not seek in every way possible to make these changes I will harass the government, and I intend to take every opportunity to do this. It can be done by one person. I am not asking for the support of anyone.
I do not think the rules are as good as they could be. I am not suggesting the changes I have in mind are the best, but I have not talked to anyone who agrees that taking away this supper hour will add nothing to the efficiency of the House of Commons. It will do nothing for the staff except create new appointments which really, would not be necessary if we were to revert to the old order of business.
I hope the government will consider these representations and give an answer to them. The newspapers will be watching this situation and they will be as hard on the government as they will be on the rest of us. On every occasion when the government fails to raise a quorum, they will make it known. Every time the government is represented by fewer members than the opposition, the public will hear about it. If this is the way in which they intend to operate in future, I strongly suggest to the government that it take steps to secure better attendance. The whip will find it hard to duplicate what he
Interim Supply
did at a quarter to six. For these reasons I hope the house leaders can get together to bring about a change which I believe is long overdue.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
I, as a representative of labour, hope that some of the labour unions will take an interest in the House of Commons in the near future. I invite any of them who represent people who work in similar professions or trades to come to this house and organize the workers in it. They can do so out of my office, if they wish, and I hope the day will come when on parliament hill we can provide labour conditions that will at least be as reasonable as those provided in other industries, in other fields-yes, and even in the civil service of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that the hon. member for Timiskaming brought himself into order by some unusual procedural acrobatics, I would like to support him in what he has said because we are dealing with a labour problem right here in this house. The hon. member is quite right in saying he has not met anyone who is really satisfied with our present arrangements. I want to support his protest against sitting during the dinner hour because, in the first place, it is distinctly unfair to the staff.
The hon. member for Timiskaming speaks from the heart; he does not speak from the book. When he was speaking on external affairs the other day he made an excellent speech. He was complimented right and left and was mentioned in the press. If anyone wonders why, it is because he spoke the language of the farmers, the men who walk behind the plough, or nowadays ride behind it. He spoke the language of the miners, the men who wield the picks, and the language of the men who use their saws in the woods. He is in close touch with the people he represents and I give him every credit for that.
Even though this matter has already been dealt with this session, I would suggest that there be a reconsideration of it. I have talked to quite a number of the staff, and personally I think it is most unfair to the Hansard angels. As you know, Mr. Chairman, I never forget to mention them. I understand there is someone being trained at present, or some people who may join the staff in the future. The same is true of the interpreters, of some other sections of the staff, and of the Hansard reporters. There are also others who are affected during the dinner hour. I support the

February 7, 1966
Interim Supply
hon. member for Timiskaming wholeheartedly and I ask that some consideration be given to the staff.
Looking around at my hon. friends on the Conservative benches I may say that I understand on good authority they were largely responsible for our sitting during the dinner hour.
You have been talking to the Grits.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Your whip was pressing for it.
I understand some of their backbenchers are not in agreement with it but, Mr. Chairman, this conversation that is going on here makes it difficult for me to be heard.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The hon. member for Ontario is blaming me. I moved an amendment last session to get rid ot it.
No matter who moved what, I trust this late effort on the part of the radical section of the N.D.P. will bear fruit in the near future.

I am very much surprised at the last sentence or two from the hon. member for Kootenay West, blaming the Conservative party for the changes that have transpired in the rules. These changes were brought in by the government. The N.D.P. always supports the government and that is why we have these new rules. We were not the ones-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit a question? Was it not his leader, the leader of the official opposition, who proposed and pushed for the idea of sitting between six and eight?
Well, we certainly have heard everything now, trying to put the blame as usual on the Leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Well, isn't it the truth?

Of course he is the most prominent, and active, and able politician in Canada at the present time, but everything that happens that does not meet with the approval of my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre must be blamed on the Leader of the Opposition. Why don't you blame the government? You support the government all the time; put the blame where it belongs.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: And you supported the government on this.
To blame the Leader of the Opposition for this is simply ridiculous, but is in keeping with the attitude of the members of the N.D.P. If they blamed the government-
I was blaming the government.
-there might be some disappearance of that mutual admiration that they have for each other.
Don't include me in that appellation.

But over the years we have had the N.D.P. acting as Liberals in a hurry and now they want to put on our party, and on the Leader of the Opposition, the blame for something that was done by the Liberal government. What else do you want to blame on the Leader of the Opposition?
Let me say this about the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He was the activating force in the committee on rules that worked for a couple of years trying to change completely the nature of this institution, and we had to spend a great deal of time restraining him. He was so convinced in his own mind that his ideas in regard to parliament were so superior to anyone else's that he bamboozled the members of that committee, along with one or two other former members of the house who are no longer with us, and tried to impose his will on the House of Commons. Now he wants to blame the Leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Did I propose sitting between six and eight? I certainly did not.
No; it was a good idea.

May I just say with regard to the words of wisdom given to us by the hon. member for Timiskaming that there are certain matters he brought up that should be considered very seriously. If the members of the staff of the House of Commons are being seriously inconvenienced by the rules we have now adopted, that should be corrected and corrected immediately. That is up to the government. The committee on internal Economy can deal with this thing right away and make provision so that the staff of the House of Commons is not inconvenienced.
So far as the members themselves are concerned the rule change providing for us to sit through the dinner hour on Mondays, Tuesdays and Thursdays, and the lunch hour on Fridays, is an experiment for one session. If it does not work it can be thrown out. If it does work it should achieve the object which
February 7, 1966

so many people have been after for a long time around here, the object of shortening the sessions of parliament.
We have heard that cry year after year, but by adding eight hours per week to our sittings it should be possible to complete the business of parliament in a normal year in six to seven months. That is why the hours of sitting have been enlarged. We were sitting only 25J hours per week previously. Now it is up to 331 hours. In days gone by we found that we had to extend the hours during the last two or three weeks of the session, sit late at night, and sit on Saturdays. Those who want to abolish the present rule will have to provide some alternative so that the house sits for a longer period than 25i hours a week. That is the way I see it.
Had I not been stirred up by the members of the N.D.P. and their unfair attack on the Leader of the Opposition I would not have spoken at this length. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I see no particular purpose in prolonging the discussion of interim supply. What I wanted to do was to express my sympathy with the Minister of National Revenue who has been selected as the sacrificial lamb, or sacrificial goat for the Liberal party. If his name is recorded in the history of this institution, as I am sure it will be, attached to it forever will be the fact that he was the minister who had to come in sack cloth and ashes to the House of Commons and ask for interim supply for the eleventh month of the fiscal year.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
This is a good suit.
I express my sympathy to him.
It should have been the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Transport.

I wish it had been the Minister of Public Works, the leader of the house, or the Minister of Transport-that would have been even better-who had to come here and ask the house for interim supply. Surely the Minister of Transport should have been the one to perform this difficult task on behalf of the government. Yet, no, the poor Minister of National Revenue had to sacrifice himself for his colleagues.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of National Revenue has gained this distinction, he has set an important precedent. I should like to 23033-54
Interim Supply
let him know how important that precedent is. The Prime Minister has indicated how important it is. Let me quote the Prime Minister, who has a great understanding of parliament, when he made this statement on December 19, 1962 as recorded in Hansard at page 2834:
There is, I believe, no precedent in our parliamentary history for a government asking for the tenth monthly instalment of the total expenditures for a year before one single item of annual expenditure has been voted by parliament-not one. This is something that has not happened before in our parliamentary history.
It is a traditional and fundamental right of parliament to vote taxes before they are collected and to approve expenditures before they are made. When these rights are ignored, when they are violated, parliament itself is being violated and we are taking a step toward its destruction.
What do we now have facing us and facing the Minister of National Revenue? What does that hon. gentleman have on his shoulders now but that, to use the words of the Prime Minister, which is destroying parliament. The Prime Minister said that when these rights are ignored and violated parliament itself is being violated and we are taking a step toward the destruction of parliament. In Canada's history the Minister of National Revenue will be credited with having taken this fatal step by coming here asking for the eleventh month of interim supply. He wants a blank cheque for 11 out of 12 months of interim supply to cover the careless spending of the taxpayers' money, without an examination by parliament.
Shame.

I feel sorry for the poor Minister of National Revenue, and I regret that it was not the Minister of Transport or the Prime Minister himself who had to perform this unfortunate task.
In any event, Mr. Chairman, the precedent has been set by the Liberal party. I am pleased to see the Liberal party set precedents. It set another precedent in 1965. I have searched the records and I cannot find another instance when a government was returned to power by the people and immediately suffered the resignations of three senior cabinet ministers. That is another precedent set by the Liberal party. This government was returned to power only to see three members of the cabinet commit hara-kiri. This is the same Liberal government that is destroying parliament by not letting us have control over government expenditures.
No wonder there has been a change in the atmosphere of this house, a change which has

February 7, 1966
Interim Supply
been noted by members of the press gallery. The change has been in the humility displayed by the treasury benches which was not evident during the last two and a half years. Those members are now quiet and subdued. The election turned out differently from what they expected and their cabinet is not as strong as it was before. Some of their supporters have had to withdraw and resign and that has made a difference in this place. Of course, Mr. Chairman, we are not people to gloat over this because it is an unfortunate thing and the great Liberal party should not be suffering so severely.
I note the Minister of Transport has taken his place. In his absence I was expressing my regret that it was the Minister of National Revenue who had to come into the house and humbly ask for interim supply for the eleventh month of the fiscal year. At that time other members suggested that the Minister of Transport would have been a more suitable individual to perform this task. I agree that it might have been better had he been the one to bear the burden for his colleagues in the cabinet, and for the Liberal party in asking for the eleventh month of interim supply and, in the words of the Prime Minister, take that step toward the destruction of parliament.
As I have stated, I see no particular purpose in prolonging the discussion on interim supply. We do not intend to do what the Minister of Transport suggested in his articles of 1962-hold up the vote on interim supply and force the government to the country. That was the irresponsible advice he gave to his party, but we are not going to do that. We do not think it would be the best means of indicating our dissatisfaction with this incompetent government with which we are saddled, to hold up interim supply and prevent cheques going out to employees of the government right across Canada.
The government got itself into this box as a result of its own actions and the Prime Minister carries the major responsibility in this regard. He was the one who called the election after telling us we were coming back in September to finish parliament's business. He called an election which did not come out the way he expected, and his cabinet began to fall apart. He could have called parliament back before Christmas but he did not. He has now had to ask his Minister of National Revenue to humbly beseech parliament to grant interim supply for the eleventh month.

We now have a precedent which will stand for all time, for which the Liberal party is responsible.

Mr. Chairman, it is very gratifying to many of us who feel that some consideration should be given to the staff of the House of Commons in respect of an appropriate break in their working day, to hear that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre strongly supports that point of view, as suggested by the remarks just made.
I believe that this committee should give endorsation to those views held by the Conservative party, to allow an appropriate supper break this evening for the staff of this house and for the 13 Liberal members who are now present.
Therefore I should like to move, based upon that support, that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, at which time the house can make an appropriate order allowing a recess for supper.
