Mr. Chairman, there are two important matters which I wanted to raise and discuss before the committee of supply,
February 7, 1966

but the appropriate ministers are not present and I have no wish to hold up this interim supply measure. I am therefore going to content myself with referring to these two matters and express the hope that when we come to the regular estimates we shall be able to get some satisfactory explanation from the government.
The first matter I want to say a word about has to do with Victor G. Spencer whose case I have raised on orders of the day frequently since the session began on January 18. I am not going to take the trouble to review his whole case at this time, except to say that in the opinion of the members of this party this man has been treated shamefully and abominably; that he is being stripped of his rights as a Canadian citizen; that first of all he was accused in a press release by the Department of External Affairs of being implicated in espionage; that later on he was named by the Minister of Justice on a national television program and it was announced that he would be kept under police surveillance for the rest of his life if he continued to live in Canada.
What is even more serious is the fact that this man was dismissed from the civil service without any right of appeal and has been deprived of his pension rights. When the hon. member for Winnipeg North asked the Prime Minister how this man could be dismissed without appeal, when the government itself had set up a committee to hear appeals of civil servants, the Prime Minister's answer was that this man's work did not have to do with security. Yet Mr. Spencer is dismissed because he is considered a bad security risk. More serious still, he was dismissed under section 50 of the Civil Service Act and denied the right of appeal to the Civil Service Commission.
The other day the Prime Minister, as reported at page 497 of Hansard, said:
-Mr. Spencer was given an opportunity to state his side of the case to-
I pause there, Mr. Chairman, because my recollection of what the Prime Minister said and my recollection of what the blues said- and I examined them quite carefully-was that Mr. Spencer was given an opportunity to state his side of the case to the Civil Service Commission, "who explained to him the circumstances that led the Post Office Department to recommend his dismissal". It has since been inserted that he "was given an opportunity to state his side of the case to a senior officer of the Civil Service Commission." The fact is, of course, that this man was
Interim Supply
never allowed to appear before the Civil Service Commission. Apparently a senior officer of the Civil Service Commission interviewed him and on this senior officer's recommendation this man was dismissed without any right of appeal.
When the estimates of the Minister of Justice come before the committee of supply I want to know whether there was a transcript of that interview with Mr. Spencer. I want to know whether Mr. Spencer was allowed to have counsel when he was being interviewed. I want to know whether he was permitted to sign any statement or whether the sole evidence of this man's unfitness to occupy the position which he held in the civil service is the statement of the senior official who interviewed him.
The other day the Minister of Justice on orders of the day said that he had looked into the matter and he was satisfied. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am not the keeper of the conscience of the Minister of Justice. If he is satisfied, then he has satisfied himself. But the laws of this country do not just require the Minister of Justice to be satisfied; they require that this house be satisfied and that the courts be satisfied-and this man has had no right of appeal either in the matter of his dismissal, his loss of pension rights, or any opportunity to prove his innocence or have his guilt determined in a properly constituted court of law.
I am not going to argue the case in any detail at this time. Both the Leader of the Opposition and members of the New Democratic party have urged the Prime Minister to appoint a judicial committee to look into this case to see whether or not this man has been deprived of his rights, has had his good name destroyed by the actions of the government and has been improperly dismissed and deprived of his pension rights.
The Prime Minister has promised to look into this matter. We are still awaiting his decision. I should like to say to the government that, while we are prepared to allow these interim estimates to pass at the present time, we shall expect a reply from the government when the estimates of the Minister of Justice come down, when we are dealing with the regular departmental estimates. We shall expect some decision from the government at that time with reference to the appointment of a judicial committee, and we shall expect some better explanation than any of the haphazard, evasive answers which we have had up to the present time.

February 7, 1966
Interim Supply
Mr. Chairman, the other matter I wanted to deal with-and, again, I shall only mention it-is the fact that I am disturbed, as I am sure every other member of the House of Commons is disturbed, on reading the report of the Auditor General. This report will undoubtedly be referred to the Public Accounts Committee; but as the Auditor General himself points out, his reports and the reports of the Public Accounts Committee have not always had too powerful an effect upon the government, and certainly have not always been reflected in government action.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
There is, for instance, the reference in the report to the fraudulent and irregular practices which have been brought to light in the administration of the winter works incentive program. There are the very glaring irregularities in the Department of National Defence with particular reference to the men who have been retired on the basis of military service stretching back to nine years of age. There has been references to irregular practices under P.F.A.A.
I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that when the regular estimates come before the house we should have the right to an explanation from each of the ministers, not only as to what has happened but as to what steps they propose to take to correct these situations. I think we might as well serve notice on the government now that we are not going to be satisfied with merely saying that the Auditor General's report will go to the Public Accounts Committee. The Public Accounts Committee will file a report to which the government may or may not pay some attention. I feel that the revelations contained in the Auditor General's report are of a sufficiently serious nature that the Committee of Supply is justified in asking for a full and complete statement from the various department affected.
We have a right to demand that the ministers tell us what action they propose to take to rectify the situation in order to satisfy the committee that there will be no recurrence of the practices which the Auditor General found so reprehensible.

When the hon. member for Timiskaming was making his remarks in respect of conditions in the House of Commons, I was reminded of the commitment the minister made that these conditions would be rectified. Just what he intends to do in that respect, I do not know.

However, I ask the minister to give consideration also to the secretarial staff and other staff members of the house in connection with the retroactive pay increases. According to a recent announcement, as I understand it, no consideration will be given to the time worked by the staff when members of parliament were away from Ottawa, a period of six or seven months. The government saw fit to keep this staff at work, and I should like to have a commitment from the minister that when the retroactive pay is being assessed the time when members were away from the House of Commons will be included.

Mr. Chairman, I know that the government is anxious to get interim supply through, but I make no apology for speaking at this time. I do not believe I have spoken in the house since last May. The question period is becoming increasingly strict, so it is difficult for a backbencher to have an opportunity to say anything. In addition, there are many questions which are not suitable for the order paper. I have a few remarks to make on one or two subjects, none of which will take very long. They are subjects which are very much in the news these days such as the centennial, that hearty perennial Canadian unity, and the question of railway passenger services.
In thinking about the centennial year, 1967, it becomes clear that the majority of Canadians never really see anything of this country except the part in which they live. They may travel 100 or 200 miles away, but the majority never see very much of Canada. For example, I wonder how many people who live in eastern Ontario have ever seen western Canada and, in particular, the beautiful province of British Columbia? I see the Minister of Transport is here. I wonder how many residents of Newfoundland have been off that island? What percentage of the total population of Canada have ever seen Newfoundland? I have not been there myself, although I am looking forward to going one of these days.
I know there are some Canadians who do not want to travel a great deal. In British Columbia there is a feeling that if you have seen the coast, then that is all that is really necessary. It seems to me that in the centennial year we should make every effort to encourage Canadians to travel to other parts of Canada. A start has already been made in this direction. The Centennial Commission has given some grants in the past three years
February 7, 1966

to what they call the youth travel plan. As a result of this plan, thousands of young Canadians have travelled across the country. People from British Columbia and Alberta have come to Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. People from the Atlantic provinces have gone to the west. If you have read accounts by those young people, what they think of other parts of the country, how interesting it was to meet people in other parts of the country, then you realize how important such a program is.
I am thinking of the average Canadian who cannot afford to travel great distances. I am thinking of the average Canadian who works for wages and has two or three weeks vacation each year. He can only go for a short holiday in an automobile. Throughout western Canada, the tendency is to cross the border and go into the northwestern United States. Here, in Ontario, the tendency is to go to New York or the New England states. We do not get to other parts of Canada.
I believe that if you want to encourage people to do this there has to be some practical help given. I suggest that the Centennial Commission should give consideration to a plan for subsidizing travel in Canada during 1967. Subsidies might be given of the sort that are now given to the young people for travel within the country. If you want the average working man in Calgary or Vancouver to go, for example, to Montreal to see Expo '67, then you have to realize he is not going to be able to do it in two weeks vacation driving an automobile. Most of this time would be spent in driving there and back and he would have no time to visit Expo or other parts of eastern Canada.
I want to suggest that serious consideration be given to subsidizing railway transportation in Canada during 1967. This may cost a great deal of money, but I believe it would be worth it. It would have several good effects. In some ways, it would contribute to this thing about which we are always talking, Canadian unity. It would keep within Canada a large amount of Canadian money which is going south of the border each year to pay tourists' expenses. I know that a large amount of money might be involved, but I believe the results would be well worth it. I mention this now because this sort of thing needs a great deal of planning in advance. Railway passenger cars cannot be produced overnight; schedules cannot be arranged. We might even produce enough business by such a plan to
Interim Supply
encourage the Canadian Pacific Railway to keep the "Dominion" going.
However, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me we will not achieve this travel in Canada by Canadians from the far corners of the country unless there is some incentive from the government. This incentive would have to take the form of a subsidy of several millions of dollars toward rail transportation. If this is not done I would say that very few people from the far west will ever get to Montreal to see Expo '67. It is no small thing for a person with a family of three or four children and two or three weeks holiday to drive across the continent and meet all the expenses. If he tried to make this trip by train it would be a matter of three days each way, and if there were some fare subsidy I think he would be encouraged to do so.

Mr. Chairman, I just have two matters to raise and I think I am justified in raising them at this point. The first is in connection with the staff of the House of Commons. I am informed that the waitresses in the restaurant and cafeterias were entirely overlooked when salary increases were considered. I think this is most unfortunate.
[DOT] (8.00 p.m.)
These are some of the lower paid people. I urge the internal economy commission of the House of Commons to go into this matter to see whether this injustice cannot be corrected as soon as possible. That is item No. 1, Mr. Chairman.
The next item I wish to bring to the attention of the minister who is present, and who I know is very sympathetic to my appeal, is the question of the policy of the B.C. Hydro in relation to the purchase or expropriation of properties along the Arrow Lakes. The chairman of the B.C. Hydro, the famous Dr. Hugh Keenleyside, has indicated to his staff that on no account will they give a detailed appraisal of any property. They simply come to the property owners and the farmers and offer them so much, with a take-it-or-leave-it attitude, although they back water a bit in a number of cases.
A question arose when some business people and farmers claimed depreciation on account of their premises or their barns or other properties owned in connection with their operations, and they wanted a detailed appraisal in order to be able to assess the recapture value when it came to filing their income tax returns this year or next year. This

February 7, 1966
Interim Supply
matter has concerned them very much indeed. In fact, it is one of the reasons that the Arrow Lakes Property Owners Protective Association has been formed.
This group had a number of meetings and they finally persuaded Hon. Ray Williston to come and listen to their complaints. He spent three hours with them. They took a tape recording of what the minister said, which was a very good thing to do in the circumstances, and afterwards invited me to listen to it.
The minister in question agreed with them. He thought that B.C. Hydro should give them a detailed appraisal of their properties so that they would know what recapture there would be on their properties by way of depreciation which had been claimed in previous years.
I brought this to the attention of the minister last year, and he wrote me what I thought was a very courteous and informative letter. I informed these people of it everywhere I went, had it published in the press and also mailed out a lot of copies. This alerted a lot of them to what may happen in the future. In one instance a farmer claimed depreciation of up to $5,000 on his barn. If he accepts a certain price from B.C. Hydro without a detailed appraisal, then he may accept much less than he might if this matter were taken into consideration.
Unfortunately the minister has failed to act in this matter. I refer to the British Columbia minister, not to the Minister of National Revenue; he is lily white by comparison. Unfortunately, the minister failed to take a stand. A committee was formed, headed by a member of the Social Credit party. Its secretary is a member of our party and the rest of the committee is comprised of members from other parties. I told them they had to have a Social Credit member as chairman, so that it was completely unpartisan; and everybody knows that I speak in an unpartisan manner when I speak on questions of principle, especially moral principle.
I just raise this matter briefly tonight, Mr. Chairman, and I hope it will receive the immediate attention of the minister so that these people can be correctly advised as to the policy of the income tax branch. This will enable them to bring increasing pressure on B.C. Hydro or on the minister concerned in order to obtain a detailed appraisal of their properties, so they know where they stand in relation to any offer made to them by B.C. Hydro.
[Mr. Herridge.l

Mr. Chairman, I apologize to the committee for taking time at this moment, and I would not do so but for one factor. My remarks this evening, which will be brief, concern the Minister of National Health and Welfare. While the matter could be brought up just as well on his estimates, I see from the list that his estimates are well down and may not be reached for some time. Since it is the general understanding that the government is planning a variety of legislation to alleviate a number of evils in the field of welfare, I should like to bring this matter to the attention of the government in case it has not already been considered.
I refer in particular to the residence requirement connected with recipients of old age assistance, disabled persons allowance and the blind pension. At the present time a person is required to have 10 years residence in this country before he can receive any of these pensions. In a country such as Canada, which is so desperately looking for immigrants and needs them very badly, as everyone in the house knows, it is a very strange thing that at a time when the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is trying to get people to come to Canada our legislation discriminates against them.
In the province of Ontario, where the widows pension is paid entirely by the province without federal assistance, the residence requirement is only one year. On the other hand, in the case of old age assistance, disabled persons allowance and the blind pension, to which the federal government contributes a very substantial amount, laying down the regulations in connection therewith, 10 years residence is required. Therefore if the minister or the government are planning any legislation to remedy some of these anomalies, I suggest this is one matter which should be given very careful consideration.
The other matter I wish to raise concerns the requirements for those who apply for disabled persons allowance. I am sure every member of this house regardless of party has constantly run into the problem of the person who is disabled, cannot work, cannot make any money, and is turned down for disabled persons allowance because he cannot meet the requirement that he be totally and permanently disabled. Under the present interpretation of the requirements, and under instructions from the government, a person practically has to have both arms and both legs off before he is eligible for this pension.
February 7, 1966

This seems to me ridiculous. I am sure every hon. member knows of case after case of persons really in need of this pension, being unable to work and eventually ending up on municipal relief of some sort. These people should get the pension but do not.
I would suggest to the government that if in fact they are giving consideration to this sort of circumstance two requirements might be met, and these regulations accordingly changed. One is that you cannot have everyone applying for this type of pension. There should be some basic requirement, such as that a person has been disabled for 12 months. It seems to me that the present requirement that a person be totally and permanently disabled is very difficult to meet, particularly as some doctors are really rigid with regard to signing certificates to this effect. Therefore it seems to me that unemployability should be the criterion to apply in deciding whether to grant a pension.
As long as a person is in the condition of being unemployable, or is unable to seek employment and make a living, he or she should receive this pension. There should be, let us say, a 12-month disability period as a basic requirement. Unemployability should be the criterion, not the strange, rigid rule presently applicable-namely that a person has to be totally and permanently disabled.
I think the present regulation is an iniquitous one which has worked great hardship on many people, as I am sure all hon. members know. If the government is planning legislation in this regard I certainly hope they will give consideration to a new criterion, namely that a person be substantially disabled and not able to work. I think this would be a more realistic approach to the matter.

Mr. Chairman, I regret that the Minister of Transport has just been called out of the chamber because I wanted to tell him that I was one up on the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, who was speaking a few minutes ago, in that I did have an opportunity of visiting the beautiful constituency of Bonavista-Twillingate, which the minister represents in this house, and that I had indeed climbed to the top of the lighthouse tower of Cape Bonavista.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I am sure, Mr. Chairman, you probably realize that my principal reason for rising is not to talk about the glories of that constituency, or indeed of any other at this moment. What I wish to do, Mr. Chairman, is to tell
Interim Supply
the Minister of Transport that when his departmental estimates are called I, as one member of this house, want to hear from him something further on the subject of the exclusion from the recently announced shipbuilding subsidies of ships built for a provincial government. I shall want to hear more than we have so far heard from the government side.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words on the subject of Southern Rhodesia. I expressed my thoughts on the Viet Nam situation the other day but I do not think enough attention has been paid by the committee to the problem created by the actions taken by Southern Rhodesia and by Canada in the current situation.
I support the criticism of the hon. member for Oxford of the method by which the government has approached this problem. I regret that the Secretary of State for External Affairs did not at the opening of this session of parliament present us with a white paper, setting out the facts concerning Southern Rhodesia. He had time to prepare one, all November, all December and part of January, and it would have been very helpful to us.
I also regret that the minister did not present a resolution to the house asking the approval of parliament for the action taken
[The Chairman.]

by the government. Now in a roundabout way he is attempting to get the approval of the house for his actions. As recorded at page 700 of Hansard for February 3, speaking about Southern Rhodesia, the minister said:
That is what is involved in this problem and that is why the government has taken the position it has. That is why I am asking this house, by the reaction it takes to these measures, to clearly indicate that the course we have taken in support of Britain, and other Commonwealth countries, with the aid of countries outside the Commonwealth, was a course of wisdom, a course of courage and a course that represents a necessary development of our foreign policy.
How does the minister get the approval or disapproval of the house by that method? The normal procedure is to divide the house, if it wishes to divide, or have a resolution placed in front of it so that a decision can be reached one way or the other. Is the minister going to interpret the things that have been said here as representing the approval by the house of his wisdom and courage in his conduct of our foreign policy? I am not at all sure that I approve of any wisdom on his part, and I am not sure where the courage comes in. What is the danger that would call forth courage under these circumstances?
Now and again the minister gets off into the stratosphere and I would like to bring him down to earth. He bases his case for the action taken by the government on the Export and Import Permits Act, sections 3(c) and 5(c) which permit the act to be applied in circumstances "to implement an intergovernmental arrangement or commitment," and he has placed in front of us an exchange of letters between Canada and Great Britain.
It may well be that technically he can base his case on that exchange of letters and on those sections of of the act, but I suggest to him that the act was never intended for the purpose for which he has used it. If the minister referred to Hansard for 1947 he would find set out in it the reasons for the drawing up of that act and its presentation to the house. It was drawn up as a modification of the War Measures Act.
In 1947 parliament was trying to divest itself of the excessive powers which were necessary in wartime. One of the problems that faced the government of the day was the question of what to do when there was a scarcity of essential goods, when countries around the world were looking for some of the materials and foodstuffs available in this country, and when Canada itself was looking for materials and supplies from other countries. So an arrangement was worked out
February 7, 196G	COMMONS
whereby control was vested in the government by virtue of the Export and Import Permits Act.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
The purpose of the act is set out very clearly, and those who are interested may look at Hansard of February 18, 1947, pages 568 to 569. I will just read what the then minister of trade and commerce said on that occasion, and I quote:
While the main purpose of the export control is to ensure adequate supply in Canada, the export controls are also necessary to enable us to carry out Canada's commitments in connection with those foodstuffs which are in world short supply and which, by common agreement of the united nations, must be formally allocated to ensure an equitable distribution.
He then stated:
A similar situation arises in connection with the carrying out of our food contracts with the United Kingdom. A third type of control which is envisaged by this measure is that relating to the movement of arms, munitions and war materials and supplies.
That was the situation in 1947. Similarly, import controls were introduced into the act in order that goods brought into Canada that were in short supply might be allocated among those firms, corporations or individuals who required them, without anyone cornering the market.
In 1954 that act was rewritten and brought up to date, and the controls were continued. In 1954 a section (c) to paragraph 3 and paragraph 5 was introduced. If one reads the debates of 1954 he will find some comment with regard to that particular section. I will give you the citation as it appears on March 18, 1954 at page 3140. At that time the committee of the whole house was discussing clause 3(c) and Mr. Donald Fleming said:
-what governmental arrangements... are now in existence?
Mr. Dickey, who was the parliamentary secretary to the minister of trade and commerce replied:
The only one... Is the United Nations resolution relating to the shipment of arms and materials of war to red China.
I submit, sir, that the Export and Import Permits Act was devised to control very largely the exports from this country of materials that might be used for war purposes and, on the import side, to be used in case the Canadian economy was disrupted by an influx of goods that were not needed, particularly agricultural products. One might think in terms of butter, turkeys, small fruits and so on.

This brings us to the present time. The minister has extended the use of this act to impose economic sanctions against Rhodesia. I think he has misused the act because it was never intended for that purpose. Of course it was intended to prevent the supply of comfort to enemy nations, by preventing their purchase of military supplies in Canada. In troubled or sensitive areas of the world, as external affairs calls them, war materials should not be supplied.
The minister has attempted to rely on what was done in respect of South Africa a couple of years ago when the export to South Africa of military supplies was prohibited. He used a rather strange example and said that trucks were not permitted to be exported from Canada because they might be used for military purposes. That sounded a bit ludicrous because all sorts of things can be used for military purposes. One could use bicycles, motorcycles, hand carts or wheelbarrows in times of war for military purposes. However, the act was used then to prevent the export of trucks from Canada. I am not at all sure that that was a wise use of the act. However, he built his case on this and said that this was a progression and that we had now reached the stage, based upon this example from the past, where we could use the act for sanction purposes against Rhodesia.
I am in complete agreement with the concept that military supplies should not be sent to Rhodesia, because it has become a sensitive area; but I think it is wrong to impose sanctions against Rhodesia by the use of this act. The proper step and the one that should have been taken would be by resolution to this house and approval by parliament before any action was taken. If action had to be taken rapidly, then there should have been subsequent validation of that action by parliament.
In this case the government has used arbitrary power-government by order in council. It has neglected parliament. When we were in opposition in the years of 1952, 1953, 1954, 1955 and 1956 we were fighting the battle of arbitrary control, fighting the battle of government by order in council, and we had many interesting debates on that subject. The government now has slipped back into this use of controls without reference to parliament. I give fair warning to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that when the Export and Import Permits Act comes up for review by July of this year we will attack his misuse of this act, and his

Mr. Chairman, I am not suggesting that the minister could not obtain support for his policy with regard to Rhodesia had he brought a resolution forward. I think the House of Commons might have agreed with him. On the other hand we should have been given an opportunity to discuss the matter, allowing those who do not agree with his policy to register that disagreement.
I should now like to draw the minister's attention to another subject. Why did the minister not set out before parliament the five principles on which Great Britain and Rhodesia attempted to come to terms before that fatal day of November 11 when unilateral action was taken by Rhodesia? Why did he not set out those five principles and allow us to consider them? Why did he not suggest to us that our aim at this time is to reopen negotiations with Rhodesia? Why did he withdraw our trade commissioner in Southern Rhodesia? What harm was he doing there. He has left an international commissioner in Viet Nam, which is costing us hundreds of thousands of dollars, and he suggests that we still have a chance to talk with opposition forces in an attempt to get them to negotiate, but with this sister country within the commonwealth he immediately withdraws our only point of contact, the trade commissioner.
Mr. Chairman, I think the action taken by the minister is wrong in regard to Southern Rhodesia and the withdrawing of the trade commissioner there. We now have no one with whom we can keep in contact to obtain a clear picture of the situation there.
I suggest the minister has failed to give us a proper outline of the attitudes that have been set forth in other parliaments within the commonwealth. He might have related to us the full story in respect of the debates in the House of Commons at Westminster, the full description of the attitudes taken by the premier of New Zealand and by the former premier of Australia. Why should we not have received a picture as clear as the picture presented in those countries ?
A day or two ago when the Leader of the Opposition was speaking in this house he asked this question, as recorded at page 753 of Hansard of February 4, 1966:
What right have the other nations of the Commonwealth then, at the prime ministers' conference to say to a colonial country under the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom: This is the course you shall follow . . .


What authority has the prime ministers' conference of the nations of the commonwealth to say this thing has got to stop, when it is a matter exclusively within the jurisdiction of one of the nations of the Commonwealth?
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I notice that Prime Minister Sir Robert Menzies of Australia expressed a similar point of view. This comes from one of the most experienced prime ministers within the Commonwealth. I quote from a press release received in Ottawa on January 18:
We have taken our decisions on this matter on a ground of important principle, adherence to which is in our opinion of the greatest importance to the long term future and interests of Australia and of the Commonwealth. We put them in this order because-
1.	Our prime duty is to Australia.
2.	If the modern Commonwealth, on the initiative of some or many of its members, begins to claim the right to intervene in and give orders in relation to matters which are the proper concern of some individual member of the Commonwealth, good relations cannot long continue, nor can the present Commonwealth structure long endure.
This is something to which we have to give the greatest and most serious consideration. Have we set a precedent now by which Commonwealth countries are going to interfere with other Commonwealth countries? Some time in the future will Commonwealth countries join together and raise trouble with Canada over something we are doing that is within our own internal jurisdiction? I doubt very much whether the course that has been pursued has been wise.
I should like now to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs, what attitude is he going to take for the future? He has told us what has been done. There has been escalation of the controls-this escalation has been in about four stages now-imposed against Rhodesia by the nations of the Commonwealth and around the world.
These controls started off with the withdrawal of the Commonwealth preferences and certain restrictions on sterling; then certain export and import controls were imposed, then controls in respect of oil, and just the other day the minister advised us that practically 100 per cent export and import controls had been imposed on Canada's part. So there has been an escalation of the action taken with regard to Rhodesia.
What if these controls fail? This is where I hope the minister will give some guidance to the house. My reason for asking him that question is based upon two grounds. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard when speak-
February 7, 196B	COMMONS
ing the other day in the debate said, as reported at page 727 of Hansard:
1 had hoped it would be made clear to Spain, Portugal and South Africa that should they not join with the rest of us in the imposition of sanctions we are prepared to impose sanctions against them also.
I do not know whether the hon. member was speaking with the knowledge and support of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but he is an important member on the government side and the minister had better tell us whether or not what the hon. member said meets with his approval. At page 728 the hon. member went on to say:
If sanctions do not work, then the only and ultimate weapon, may I say, that the international community has at the moment is force and the use of force.
He said further on:
Therefore it is important for us and for all the countries of the world that we should be determined in this instance to see that these sanctions work.
How are we going to make sure that these sanctions work; and if they fail, are we going to resort to force? The hon. member for York South made the usual fluent speech that he makes in this house. I listened to him without much trouble. I find he is easy to listen to, but I always examine what he has to say with the greatest care because he can lull you into fault. He was talking the other day about what I would call the blood bath theory. He led us to believe in the course of his remarks that what is happening in some of the developing countries of the world is a replica of what has happened to nations with a long history.
He recalled to our minds that our ancestors went through centuries of bloodshed in order to establish their freedom and he left the impression with me that we should immediately withdraw from any involvement in Africa and let the people there fight it out. I think that is a wrong thing to suggest in this century and I was surprised that the Secretary of State for External Affairs did not immediately answer the hon. member for York South. The minister gave me the impression that he rather approved of some of the things the hon. member was saying, and I think it is high time the minister told us whether or not he did approve of those remarks.
That brings me in the five or six minutes I have left, Mr. Chairman, to this question. How far is the minister prepared to go? His government has imposed economic sanctions

Ii there is not a quick kill, if the sanctions fail, what are we to do? The Prime Minister of Great Britain, pressed on this point, said that there would not be the application of force. However, we have people in this house suggesting that force should he applied. Now, what does the minister say to that? Are we going to advocate or support the use of force against Southern Rhodesia if it does not yield under the circumstances?
Against Ian Smith, not Southern Rhodesia?

Well, against Ian Smith; but if you use force against the government of Ian Smith you will come into conflict with the people of Southern Rhodesia because I judge he has a great deal of support there. Have we calculated the effect of economic sanctions on the general populace of Southern Rhodesia? I believe Mr. Ian Smith has said that if massive unemployment results from the imposition of sanctions, the people who will feel the effect are the men who are working in Southern Rhodesia but who are not native residents of that country, who come from adjoining areas. They will be sent home, and they number in the thousands.
Are we looking for the economic collapse of Southern Rhodesia? If economic collapse occurs, then would you not be approaching a situation of anarchy? I hope the minister will deal with this point. I wish I had more time to elaborate on these points, but I want to close on this note. No matter what we may feel about the action that was taken by Mr. Ian Smith in Southern Rhodesia, no matter how virtuous we may feel about having launched into the imposition of sanctions against that country, what is the ultimate aim and how are we to achieve that ultimate aim?
Surely the ultimate aim we are after is to bring back Mr. Ian Smith's government of Southern Rhodesia into our community of nations within the Commonwealth. This can be achieved only through negotiations and compromise by either side. Surely under these circumstances the Canadian position should be leadership along that line. There is no point in saying that this is the sole responsibility of Great Britain, because we have rushed in behind the government of Great Britain and imposed sanctions. Having done that, we are entitled I would think to talk to the government of Great Britain as well as the government of Ian Smith in Rhodesia.

Is there not an opportunity here for Canada to play an important part? Should we not have some representative in Southern Rhodesia who can keep in contact with the situation there? The minister talks about negotiations being essential in so far as Viet Nam is concerned, as well as other trouble spots in the world. It is just as essential with regard to Southern Rhodesia. It would be in the interests of the white population of that country as well as the African population if a peaceful settlement could be arrived at. It is difficult to see how that can be done by this stand-offish method, this arm's length method, of the imposition of total sanctions against that country; the withdrawal of our representative; the cutting off of our aid which must have been helping the African population, and saying there is nothing we can do. I hope there will be no bloodshed in Southern Rhodesia. I hope that there will not be complete economic collapse because that will bring hardship to most of the people of Southern Rhodesia. I hope the good offices of Canada may be used in order to bring a peaceful settlement of the problem.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that all of us in this house, as well as millions of people across the world, are watching with anxious concern the results of the initiative which has been undertaken by His Holiness the Pope in trying to bring together the neutral nations in a summit conference at Geneva in order to mediate the Viet Nam war. I hope these negotiations will be successful, and I hope tremendously that Canada will be one of the first nations to respond to this call. The Minister of External Affairs has assured us that we are an independent nation in the full sense of the word. I do hope that this government will prove this is so by being ready to do whatever a neutral nation can do and should do if this summit conference becomes a reality.
The secretary general of the United Nations, U Thant, is doing the same sort of thing. Somehow we have got to the stage now where, regardless of which authority attempts to get a conference convened, we shall have to go along. Many of us recall the uneasy months prior to the outbreak of world war II and have a dreadful feeling of familiarity, as though we have been through all this before, as step by step we seem to be getting closer to the brink of disaster. I hope that this time wiser counsels are going to prevail and, regardless of the rights or wrongs on either
February 7, 19S6

side of this war, the killings, bombings and maiming of people have got to be stopped.
There is a point of no return. Once we reach that point of no return we shall be in for a war so terrible that the imagination is just staggered at the thought of it. Inevitably, there would be a war along class lines, the have and have-not nations of the world, and along colour lines. I do not know that we even dare to contemplate the results of a struggle of that kind.
I do not want to deal at any length with the war in Viet Nam. My colleagues have dealt very ably indeed with the points at issue. I should like only to express my most urgent thoughts about the present situation by reading a paragraph from a speech delivered last May in the United States congress by the Democratic representative from Oregon, Edith Green. She said this:
For many, many months now I have searched for every possible excuse to support my government in the policies it is pursuing in Viet Nam- and I have supported it. In spite of the shaky "domino" theory, I have done my very best to believe in it; in spite of the fact that the people of South Viet Nam have been subjected to one unpopular and unstable dictatorship after another, I have done my best to believe we are defending their freedom; in spite of the fact that we have violated the Geneva accords, I have done by best to believe this was justified because the North Vietnamese did also, even though I know that two wrongs do not make a right; in spite of one humiliating military defeat after another, I have done my best to believe all the optimistic reports about our really winning the war over there; in spite of all the evidence of internal discord and revolt against the governments we maintain in power, I have done my best to believe this is what the Vietnamese people really want us to do but, my fellow Americans, there is a point beyond which credibility simply will not stretch-and it is that somehow by waging a wider war we pursue a policy of peace.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I think we have got to the stage beyond which that credibility will stretch no longer. Today I feel that somehow the United States government must be dissuaded from its policy of widening the war in Viet Nam. It is not the business only of the United States government, it is the business of the whole world. Today it is not a case of being antiAmerican but being pro-human race when we urge that this war be brought to a close. That is why I feel that all of us must welcome with a hope born of great dread the initiative of Pope Paul.
Actually, we will never know what real freedom from war in the world is until we get down to the job of giving the United Nations the power to make and to maintain
Supply-External Affairs peace, no matter who the belligerents may be. We cannot forget that after 20 years of existence the predecessor of the United Nations 

incidentally the United Nations reaches its twenty first birthday only this year-the league of nations, gave up the ghost. And why? For one reason and one reason only -because it could not make the peace. Nobody else could either, but the league of nations was unable to make the peace. War came and the league of nations was its first casualty.
The United Nations has great achievements to its credit in economic, social and cultural fields. No one needs to be reminded of the tremendous job it has been doing in all of these fields and for people all around the world. But I am absolutely sure that unless the United Nations can somehow get over the hurdle of peace making and peace keeping and can come to grips with these tasks, it is going to fail as miserably as did the league of nations; and it will go up in the flames of world war III as surely as the league of nations went up in the flames of world war II.
This is why it is so imperative at this time to try to see what can be done to build the United Nations. You may say that it is too late for that kind of thing. I say no, it is not. We have seen one difficulty after another arise. If we get out of Viet Nam by hook or by crook then another situation will develop, and yet another and another. Sooner or later we will just have to accept the fact that the United Nations is the only organization with the world authority and with the moral authority to keep the peace and to make the peace.
We have seen that in the past Canada has been active in trying to pioneer along this road of peace making and peace keeping. A few years ago we in Canada were all very proud when the present Prime Minister, who was then Secretary of State for External Affairs, took the lead among the nations at the United Nations during the very difficult Suez crisis. He was instrumental in establishing some peace keeping machinery which really worked and which helped the world to avoid the danger of war at that time. You may say that he had the support of the big powers, Russia and the United States, behind the scenes, and so he did; but he had the nerve and the courage and the imagination to go ahead and to propose a peace keeping solution. The other nations of the world came along and supported it. We were in his debt then, as was the whole world.

February 7, 1966
Supply-External Affairs
I think we need a return to that spirit now, and need it very badly. The nations of the world have to have leadership, and I think Canada is the country that could and should give that leadership. As I say, the world needs to pioneer the idea that only the United Nations can and should be the peacemaker and the peace maintainer. We have to create the proper climate and convince all peoples that the United Nations can play this role.
That is why I for one am less than enthusiastic about a whole lot of these regional pacts. I think we are putting our trust and our confidence into something which is really only a halfway house and is not going to be able to meet the test of time. I think we have got to the stage where we have to believe that the United Nations is the authority in the world and that we have to put our weight behind it, if indeed the United Nations is going to be made to work. With courage and self-confidence Canada could give a lead. Canada could and should put forward, and work for, definite proposals openly and clearly, regardless of what any other nation thinks about them.
I realize that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has his own private opinions, which as a matter of fact he has stated domestically within Canada, along a number of these lines. But he just does not state them openly and clearly on the floor of the United Nations. I should like him to support these opinions there, because I think he would get the backing of the Canadian people who are waiting for a lead and are wanting to lead.
I am going to mention four proposals which I think should have very high priority if Canada were able to give a lead on the floor of the United Nations. First, I think Canada should propose that the United Nations should now create a permanent peace keeping system ready to act in the first stages of trouble, no matter who are the belligerents or how powerful they are.
All right, so you are not listened to when that proposal is brought before the United Nations the first few times. I have been a member of an opposition all my political life and have seen things advocated by the opposition taken over by others and turned into legislation. Gradually ideas grow and are found to be worth while. Other people take them over and turn them into legislation.
If Canada would agitate and agitate and agitate, both in season and out, for ideas like the United Nations creating a permanent peace keeping machine to which all nations

would make a contribution, I believe we could gain the support of the people of a lot of non-aligned nations, like the Scandinavians, the Africans and a lot of the Asians for such a proposal.
I see the minister looking at me as though I do not know what is going on down there. Maybe this sort of thing has been going on but Canadians have not heard enough about it. We have not got to the point of pushing and working for this thing because we have not been given a strong enough lead in the United Nations itself.
Second, I think Canada should propose that the United Nations should prohibit any member nation from taking military measures against any other country for any reason whatever. If we are serious about the United Nations being the keeper of law and order, we can no longer afford to have a world in which any nation is allowed to run and help another nation on its own without first going to the United Nations for support and for authorization. I think we have gone past the time when this is a safe procedure. I believe Canada should advocate that henceforth only the United Nations should be the peace maintainer and that other nations should work through it, instead of unilaterally helping their allies and that kind of thing.
I know these proposals may seem far out, Mr. Chairman, but they will not seem far out if we work for them. They are essential to our survival.
Third-again this proposal will seem far out to some people, but I think it is essential-the United Nations should declare now that bombing human beings is an act of savagery which must not be tolerated in the modern world. I do not care who does the bombing or who the human beings are. I do not care whether this sounds like a fantastic fairy tale.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I can point to a series of very fine lectures given in the hall of the General Assembly itself during world co-operation year where, over and over again eight lecturers from eight different countries pointed out, and I wish to point this out today, that there is only one race in the world, which is the human race, that when you bomb and maim other people you will be bombed and maimed in turn, and you will be bombing and maiming yourself. Today there are no different races. There are just different places where different kinds of human beings live.
In the fourth place I believe that the United Nations should now amend its charter
February 7, 1966

to admit all nations regardless of what kind of governments they have, and regardless of whether we like them or not. One thing I should like to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs do is to go boldly into the United Nations and say that it is time we admitted mainland China, and that we do not care who hears us say it.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that in various places within Canada. I should like to hear him say that loudly and clearly within the United Nations itself. I am convinced that I am speaking for the majority of the Canadian people when I say that. I should like to see a poll taken on that. We cannot afford outlaws in the world community of nations. I think Canada is in a peculiarly useful and fortunate position to do the sort of pioneering along the lines that I am talking of, and for a couple of reasons. First of all, we are all told and we all believe that Canada has a great fund of respect among the nations of the world. I think that we have that position throughout the world. I believe it will entitle us to ensure that we get a hearing for this sort of thing within a measurable time, because we have had experience in pioneering in this country. I do not think that anybody who recalls the history of this country will really think that what I suggest is so utterly impossible.
That is especially so when we think of how the pioneers came to this country and envisaged the idea of setting up a country with the breadth and the diversity of this land, geographically, and in every other way. When we think of the early pioners and what they had to go through, it staggers the imagination. I never go through the Rockies, through those spiral tunnels and through the Connaught tunnel without thinking of what imagination and daring it took on the part of the pioneers, and the pioneer statesmen, to do that kind of thing. This country itself is a triumph of pioneering over obstacles of one sort or another. Today we are triumphing over the difficulties of our constitution, difficulties between groups of peoples in different jurisdictions, and so on.
I should like to see Canada go at this time, and try pioneering in the United Nations once again. Let us see if we could not evoke a response from a great many peoples and from a great many countries of the world. We have got to do it, and I believe Canada is the country best fitted to carry this out.
Mr. Chairman, I like to feel that these constructive ideas can be carried forward, in
Supply-External Affairs spite of the very great difficulties which I know the Secretary of State for External Affairs has met and is meeting in the United Nations.

speechtext: I wonder if the hon. lady will allow a question. I was interested in her remarks, and particularly in her approbation of the efforts of His Holiness Pope Paul in bringing about a solution in the problem that exists. I wonder if we should not have clarification from the minister in regard to exactly where Canada stands. After all, I believe that His Holiness the Pope asked for neutral or uncommitted countries to participate. I wonder if the minister would inform us and the house exactly what position we are in.

I do
not know whether that is a question or a suggestion. In either case I should be very happy to ask the minister for an answer.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I should be very happy to give an answer. On that particular subject, as I said last week, Canada strongly supports the appeal made by the Holy Father. We note with satisfaction that, in the resolution proposed by Mr. Goldberg in the Security Council, there is an offer to utilize the neutral nations of the world as an arbitral body to consider the dispute in Viet Nam. Canada strongly supports that initiative. I sincerely hope that Hanoi and Peking will find it possible to modify their rejection of this proposal as put forward last Friday.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: I should like to have that made clear. Does the minister consider we are in that category?
Canada would be very happy to participate in this initiative.

Mr. Chairman, I was
prompted to enter this debate after I had heard the speech of the hon. member for York South. I believe at that time he said he was speaking on behalf of the New Democratic party. I sincerely hope that he was not. I am quite sure that the hon. member for Kootenay West does not go along with what he said, because I believe that the words uttered were the most subtle pieces of communist propaganda that I have ever heard since I came to this house. I will refer to his speech in a few moments.
I regret, Mr. Chairman, along with many other members of this house Canada's reluctance to enunciate a policy on many issues

February 7, 1966
Supply-External Affairs that are facing the world today. As a result of this lack of policy it leaves the Canadian people in the dark as to Canada's position in most of these issues which have been brought up in the debate. In fact, I would go so far as to say that the government seems to have no direction in regard to foreign policy. Many of us think that the government seems to straddle the fence on practically all issues. I had not intended to say this, but it was the previous speaker who brought up the subject of the Suez canal, which was the start of this foreign policy followed by the present government, or the party that is in power at this time. They started it.
I well remember the debate on the issues, and I am not too sure but that that was one of the debates that made me a stronger Conservative than I was even before that time. I remember the remarks of the Canadian delegation at that time, which strongly supported the United States stand, along with Australia and New Zealand. However, when it came to the vote, New Zealand and Australia, although they had talked against Great Britain said that, because of their Commonwealth ties, they were compelled to support Great Britain.
What did the Canadian representative do? Canada was a country that we were very proud of. The Canadian representative made a very forceful speech. At the end of it, the member representing the Canadian delegation said: "I abstain". I do not think I was ever more ashamed of Canada than I was then. I shall have more to say about the word "ashamed" in a few moments. I do not want to say too much about it because my time is restricted.
It appears to me also that the attitude of this government, and particularly that of the Secretary of State for External Affairs is that we, as Canadians, fear to stand up and be counted. Why do we take this attitude? The minister appears to be afraid to make a commitment on behalf of Canada. Might I suggest that by his silence with respect to Canadian foreign policy the minister is undermining Canada's reputation abroad.
As members of this House of Commons, we ask ourselves what is the reason for this lack of policy on the part of the government? The minister seems reluctant to inform the house of facts that he surely must have in his possession, or should have in his possession. May I suggest to him that his failure to inform the house is also a reflection-and I

hate to say this-on the staff of his department. We might well wonder whether he is concealing information. On the other hand, are the members of his staff unaware of what is actually taking place in their parts of the world? Surely the Canadian public and we, as members of this house, have the right to expect some positive policy statement from our minister. We ask what is the government policy for example, with regard to Viet Nam and with regard to Rhodesia? These questions have been asked. What is Canada's stand on support to NATO? What is the stand respecting the admittance of red China to the United Nations, and to Canada's joining the Organization of American States?
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I wonder, as did the member for Winnipeg South Centre tonight, why a white paper was not published on some of these issues. This would help to clarify the debate that has taken place in the house. It would also assist in informing the Canadian people, something which I believe should be done by the minister in charge of this department. To date, all I have gathered from the minister is that there is confusion within the Liberal cabinet on these points. I am not the only one who is of this opinion. It would appear to me that the hon. gentleman has failed to convince his colleagues as to what policy Canada should follow, or gain acceptance of any policy he has proposed. Possibly the government has adopted a policy of "wait and see" or of straddling the fence, as I have suggested, or of stalling. The hon. gentleman should let us know what the policy is.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Does he agree with the policy of the government of Canada on Rhodesia?

I will come to that in a moment.
When the Secretary of State for External Affairs was asked about the policy on the Organization of American States-and was asked by the Leader of the Opposition, to give his views on this subject, he said he had already done so. My hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition then continued his speech, taking the minister's views as being the policy of the government. The minister then got up to say: "I did not say that, I just said I believe that." So we do not know what the policy is. The hon. gentleman makes a statement and denies it later. If he does not deny
February 7, 1966

it, the Prime Minister does. The hon. gentleman should let us know what the trouble is. He should tell us why he cannot make these statements. Then, at least, he would have our sympathy.
The hon. member has lost his place.

No, but I see my time is coming to an end and there is much I should like to say. For instance, I have a good deal to say about Canada joining the O.A.S. Let it suffice, however, to say that I agree with everything my hon. friend from Oxford said the other day. I wish to add two further points. I think the minister should tell us how many of the members of that organization-20 I believe-have paid their dues. Another point which occurs to me is this: What would the attitude of the minister have been had Canada been a member of the O.A.S. during the last world war when the policy followed by that organization was one of neutrality? I suggest there has been an admission by the minister that he is not allowed to speak for his department, and this presents us with a peculiar situation.
I believe Canada's basic thought in formulating foreign policy should be "world order with freedom". We must ask ourselves how this should be achieved. To begin with, I think most of us would agree that all racism is evil; that tyrannies are reprehensible; all inequalities must be remedied and that all individuals should have the same rights, commensurate with their responsibilities. Canada took a positive step in this regard in the advance toward world order with freedom when she joined NATO. Sir Winston Churchill said not long after the Korean war: "The world today is peering around the rim of hell." Certainly, one look at the international situation today would seem to verify his statement. We can only wonder what the situation would be had the NATO alliance not been formed. I am convinced-though I can only speak hypothetically-that this alliance did prevent a third world war. I will go further and say that if such an alliance had been in existence sufficiently early the first and second world wars would never have taken place.
I arrived at these conclusions after representing our party on a tour of NATO installations last fall. I should like to state clearly that I believe the Canadian people have received full value for their support of the NATO alliance. The question in our minds
Supply-External Affairs now must be: What is Canada's attitude to NATOs future? Does Canada agree with the theory put forward by the French General Gallois that nuclear weapons have made alliances obsolete? What is Canada' assessment of de Gaulle's policy regarding the future of NATO?
Canadian policy should also be declared on the situation in Viet Nam. I should like to know how great is the threat presented by red China to the security of Australia, one of our partners in the Commonwealth. A white paper should be issued on this subject. Does the minister have in his possession information to the effect that red China has designs on this territory? I might add at this time that I am one who is opposed to red China's joining the United Nations, particularly while she insists on laying down the conditions under which she would join.
The United States has made a commitment which must be kept. If the United States did not live up to the agreements it has made with countries such as Formosa, for example, I think that never again would one of these minor countries respect the word of a major power. Although I am not pro-American I think it is Canada's responsibility to do everything she can to support the United States attitude in this respect.
I believe the answer to the question about China which I asked earlier would give the Canadian people the information they are seeking with regard to the Viet Nam conflict. An answer stating that Canada must remain silent because we are a member of the peace commission is, I suggest, not sufficient. As far as I know, that is exactly what the minister has been saying.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have been following the hon. member's interesting statement. Does he mean he would have Canada commit troops to the current conflict in Viet Nam?

Let us not fool ourselves, Canada is not a military power. I agree with what the minister has said. We are spread pretty thin with the commitments we have already made. I have no more to say on that subject. But if need be I would be prepared to support the commitment of Canadian troops. A surprising answer, isn't it?
Earlier, I said I believed the speech of the hon. member for York South to be the most subtle piece of communist propaganda I had ever heard in this house. I wish to refer to a few of his remarks. At one point he said: "I

February 7, 1966
Supply-External Affairs make no apologies about having doubts with regard to imperialistic or empire activities." I find that hard to reconcile with the rest of his speech. It seems to me he was supporting the actions of his friend Harold Wilson all the way. But he was apologizing.
Perhaps he is a communist, too.

Could be.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
In referring to one Conservative member's statement about time being required to give the African people an opportunity to learn the ways of democratic government, the hon. member for York South referred to the "whites" as if the name "whites" was a dirty word. At one time he said he had no apologies for saying he had no patience with this "white man's burden" kind of argument. Might I say to him there would be more peace in the world today if he and others like him stopped apologizing for being white.
On another occasion he said he was ashamed that a part of the British Commonwealth of Nations should have adopted policies such as the Union of South Africa had adopted. He also said he felt ashamed to be a citizen of a country that is associated with a member of the Commonwealth that had acted as Ian Smith had acted. He made no mention of being ashamed about accepting the protection these two countries provided for him during the last world war, nor is he ashamed for accepting the freedom he now enjoys because of the efforts of these two countries.
The hon. member for York South on another occasion said:
Nor is there any mystery about the repressive anti-democratic, indeed one might say neo-fascist laws which the Smith government has introduced in Southern Rhodesia.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre got up and asked the hon. member what he had to say about Russia's actions in regard to countries it has taken over. You can look up the answer in Hansard: He evaded the issue. That is the reason I said it was a very communistic type of speech. He seemed to be supporting the actions of all other types of governments that were not democratic. He used words like "anti-democratic" and "neo-fascist" in the ways we have heard them used in all communist propaganda. What did he say about Ghana? He seemed to vupport what Ghana has been doing.

Canada's position in regard to the Rhodesian question is, I believe, one that should be debated in this house. Much has been said about the unilateral and illegal actions taken by the Smith government in Rhodesia. I believe history will tell that the United States of America took similar action at one time, and so did the Union of South Africa.
Perhaps we should ask ourselves why it was that Ian Smith took this action? How did this situation develop? Could it have been avoided? Did the British Prime Minister, Harold Wilson, make a hasty and unfortunate decision for political reasons? Did he try to jump too fast into socialism?
We are told the declaration of independence was an unfortunate consequence of the dismantling of the Central African Federation headed by Sir Roy Welensky. I recently read that the Central African Federation was torpedoed by Kaunda, the present head of the Zambia government, and by Malawi, formerly Nyasaland. The article went on to say that Zambia and Malawi are rapidly moving toward one-man rule.
The slogan of majority rule has proven very useful for black leaders to prepare the way for their own autocratic regimes. So far, majority rule so ardently advocated by black leaders, has proven to be an extremely transient affair en route to one-man rule, with the same man then unblushingly explaining that parliamentary democracy is quite unsuitable to his country. Would the minister tell us if there is any evidence in his possession to deny or substantiate statements of that kind? I think this is the part of the story we have not been told.
The other day when the hon. member for York South was speaking he was asked a very sensible question by the hon. member for Oxford. He received a very facetious reply, I might say an egotistical reply. The hon. member for York South said he would be pleased at all times to educate the members of the house, and he would supply the hon. member for Oxford with a dossier of all the arguments. He seemed to think that the minister should take all his information from newspaper articles. Surely, with the amount of money we are spending on the Department of External Affairs, we must have contacts in all these countries from which we can get first hand information.
My time has almost expired, Mr. Chairman, but before I take my seat I would like to say that the government of Canada is shirking its responsibility to the Canadian people, and
February 7, 1966

also missing a golden opportunity to give leadership to the middle powers by not taking a positive stand on many of these international affairs.

Mr. Chairman, there are just a few minutes to go until ten o'clock and I hope I can complete the remarks I had intended to make before then, but the comments which we have just listened to may give me a chance to expand somewhat on what I originally intended to say.
At the outset I must say I was very much impressed by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek-
He does not care.

He does not care about anything, obviously. I was impressed by the depth of his ignorance about some extremely fundamental and basic rights of people, about the question of equality of people in other lands, and in this land as well. But all one can say about his references to the hon. member for York South, which were grossly distorted, is that this is the standard approach of those who are intolerant, those who are bigoted, those who are ignorant. It is an approach to cover one's lack of full appreciation of the rights of humanity.
I do not want unduly to elevate the hon. member's status but I would think he would fit quite properly among that rank of people who include Torquemada and the late Senator McCarthy of the United States, noted for an approach to smear by falsity, by falsification, by outright lies if necessary, in order to put across a particular point of view.
I had intended to speak about a couple of important international organizations to which Canada belongs, one being NATO and the other NORAD. Within three years it will be 20 years since Canada became a member of NATO. I think it was some time in May 1949 that the Prime Minister, who was then the Secretary of State for External Affairs, signed the NATO alliance treaty which has an initial lifetime of 20 years, after which any member nation may cease to be a member of NATO on one year's notice, or something of that sort. In any event three years hence will be the time when Canada, or for that matter any other nation, can seek to release itself of its participation in NATO.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
With respect to NORAD, which is a bilateral arrangement between Canada and the United States, it has a 10-year period of effectiveness and its expiration is in 1968. In
Supply-External Affairs this case I believe there is also a one-year notification of intention to discontinue the letters which were exchanged, and which constitute the NORAD agreement. In any event, within two years in one case and three years in the other we will be faced with having to make a decision, if a decision has not already been made, about our continuing participation in NORAD and NATO.
NATO is primarily a European structure and in its formative years was dominated by United States military and economic supremacy. It has continued to be an organization dominated by the United States, if for no other reason than that the United States, until recent years, was the most powerful military nation within NATO in possession of a nuclear capability. This position has since been challenged, notably by France, and it may well be that France will not remain in NATO within the remaining period of its life. There may, of course, be some change in this speculation in the future.
NATO was established to act as a deterrent to the westward Soviet movement, in an attempt to forestall the Soviet bloc from the taking over of countries by persuasion or by war, particularly in that western section of Europe which had been decimated by the second world war. This was a war which, apart from the results of Pearl Harbour, left the United States unscathed and in a dominant position so far as military and economic strength was concerned. Hence the United States forcefully determined the formative and continuing role of NATO.
I am particularly concerned with Article II of NATO. I understand this is the child of our Prime Minister, and that it was included in the terms of the NATO treaty upon his insistence. I am sure he recognized at that time the necessity for an economic advancement in the western world as a result of economic collaboration and co-operation. He must have seen the prospects for developing within the NATO structure an economic alliance and well-being in the North Atlantic area which would act as the greatest single bulwark against communist infiltration, which might have prevented the advancement of our growing economic system and interfered with our political democracy.
Article II has never had any great significance to NATO strategists, but it is a matter which has concerned interparliamentary conferences and various governments. However, so far as NATO itself is concerned and the council of ministers, it has been exclusively a military machine and alliance.

February 7, 1966
Supply-External Affairs
The prospects which the Prime Minister thought NATO had for economic development within its structure have wafted away with time and have been overshadowed by the military machine itself. I have thought for some years that the greatest threat, in so far as the northern hemisphere and the western portion of Europe are concerned, has existed for some time and has been an economic threat posed by the state operated economic machine that exists in the Soviet Union. We only have to look back to 1957 and 1958 to gain some idea of this fact.
In 1957-58 the aluminum industry in North America almost collapsed. The smelter at Kitimat, in my own riding, almost folded overnight. I am given to understand that actually what happened was that the Soviet Union dumped a fairly large volume of aluminum on the world market to undercut the prices. This had the effect of a depression or repression on the aluminum industry, which thought that the Soviet Union had immense quantities of aluminum for export to world markets. The fact of the matter was, as was subsequently discovered, that the Soviet Union dumped this aluminum, which it had in short supply, to drive the prices down in order that it could by one means or another purchase its requirements at prices much lower than previously existed.
That is only an example of the type of damage that can be done by the economic activities of another country. In this regard it has been recognized that the preservation of economies and freedoms in western countries has to some extent been effected by the development of economic organizations, the most notable being the common market and the O.E.C.D. These are multilateral agreements, between nations, really, that have developed within the last few years, based on a recognition that there must be this type of co-operation in order to preserve economies and democracies. To all this development Canada has been aloof in its participation. With the exception of the O.E.C.D., Canada has remained outside these developments. It has maintained its relationship primarily with the military alliances of NATO.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock.
Progress reported.
