maintopic: WATER RESOURCES-STEPS TO DEAL WITH RADIOACTIVE POLLUTION
WATER RESOURCES-STEPS TO DEAL WITH RADIOACTIVE POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last I raised a question on the floor of the house with respect to action being taken by the government on the matter of the radioactive pollution of public waters in the Elliot Lake and Bancroft areas. Your Honour's ruling was that this was a matter for the order paper and I am raising no objection to your ruling because I realize that the answer is one which might require a detailed reply. However, I subsequently

served notice in writing that I wished to bring this matter to the floor of the house at ten o'clock this evening.
Let me say at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that I am not an alarmist nor am I striving for sensationalism, but it is because of genuine concern that I am seeking an answer regarding government policy on what I consider to be an imminent and all-important issue. Two weeks ago I visited the Elliot Lake area and talked with numerous prominent citizens. At that time, I availed myself of a copy of the report entitled, "Radiological Water Pollution in the Elliot Lake and Bancroft Areas". I have given this report a great deal of study and I am firmly convinced that the situation has not been given the prominence it deserves. I find, Mr. Speaker, that there is a great area of uncertainty, and what you might call semi-contradiction, which would lead one to believe that we are lacking in research in positively defining what is a safe and what is an unsafe level of exposure to radioactive elements.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to direct your attention to an item found at the bottom of page 35 of the report to which I have just referred. In dealing with the situation in connection with radiological pollution of the Serpent river prepared by the Ontario Water Resources Commission in April, 1964, I find the report has this to say:
-that a major problem existed in the Elliot Lake area with respect to controlling radioactive contamination entering public waters. While there was no immediate hazard to health, a full investigation of the extent of the problem, and of what corrective measures could be taken, was obviously needed.
I should like now to direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, to two other quotations from the report, which in my opinion are at least a partial contradiction of the reference I have just made. On page 21, under the heading "Biological Effects", I find this:
Knowledge of the biological effects of ionizing radiation is based largely on the results of animal experiments, on clinical studies of human beings exposed during medical treatment, accident, war, or through the inhalation or ingestion of radioactive materials, and on studies of populations living in areas having a high exposure to natural 'background' radiations.
I quote from page 22 the following startling statement:
With respect to genetic effect, it is generally accepted by authorities that there is no threshold dose below which some effect may not occur.
February 7, 1S66

At this time, Mr. Speaker, I feel that I should draw to your attention one of the conclusions of the deputy ministers committee which produced this report. It was as follows:
It now appears that provincial statutes are inoperative in view of the overriding authority which is assigned to federal agencies under the Atomic Energy Control Act.
This is the prime reason I am now bringing this matter to the attention of hon. members. Following through the chronology of surveys made at numerous mine sites in both the Elliot Lake and Bancroft areas, two things seem to stand out. First, there was a lack of essential precaution in the impounding of radioactive wastes on mine property. Second, the surveys could not be properly completed on all properties because the majority of them had closed down in the period from 1960 to 1963. This leaves in my mind the very important question of what the situation might be today, had all the mines continued in full production.
I feel, as all other hon. members do, that it would be a great boon to our economy if these mines could return to full production. If and when this occurs, however, I hope that there will be no room for uneasiness or scepticism on the part of anyone with regard to the protection of citizens from a very hazardous situation. Perhaps the government is giving this matter urgent consideration. I hope this is the case. However this matter is of prime importance in the minds of many people, particularly in the minds of those who are of necessity more directly exposed. I am sure they would be grateful for assurance from the government that the matter is being given the active consideration it deserves.
Just let me reiterate, Mr. Speaker, that it is my opinion that there should be continuing research into this matter of what is a safe or unsafe level of radioactive exposure. I feel that there should be more restrictive measures with regard to the impounding of radioactive wastes.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)

speakeroldname: Mrs. Margaret Rideout (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: WATER RESOURCES-STEPS TO DEAL WITH RADIOACTIVE POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these two areas which the hon. member has mentioned are where uranium mining has been found to be economically feasible. Mining companies have been permitted to operate in these areas under federal legislation-atomic energy control regulations-but the permit covering these operations has also indicated that they would
23033-55J
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion be subject to appropriate provincial regulations.
For a number of years the Ontario Department of Health and the Ontario Water Resources Commission have collaborated in a study of the effect of these operations on public water supplies in these areas. A little over a year ago a report was released by the Ontario Water Resources Commission which showed that radioactive contamination levels in certain parts of the watershed had been found on occasion to exceed accepted permissible limits for continuous use by members of the public.
A special Ontario government deputy ministers' committee was formed to study the Elliot Lake and Bancroft area problem. The report of this committee was recently published and copies were sent to the federal government by the premier of Ontario, with a request that a meeting be convened to examine the situation and review the adequacy of existing legislation to control radioactive pollution.
A meeting was convened early in January 1966 and the extent of the pollution was carefully reviewed, as well as possible ways of controlling the pollution. Another meeting is to be held to collaborate further in the ways and means that the two levels of government can employ most effectively to find a solution to this problem.
The radiation protection division of the Department of National Health and Welfare, which is concerned with radiation and health matters nationally, has already offered assistance to the Ontario Department of Health in the form of laboratory analyses and other related radiation measurements.

maintopic: GRAIN-REPORTED INABILITY TO MAKE CERTAIN EXPORT SALES
GRAIN-REPORTED INABILITY TO MAKE CERTAIN EXPORT SALES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Finance has had to remain beyond the normal adjournment hour expressly for the purpose of answering my question I regret it very much because I realize he is busy. However, on two occasions last week I put a question to him which had to do with the matter of the movement of grain to export markets and I was not able to get a reply because of your interpretation of the rules, Mr. Speaker.
I put the question to the minister now, because I feel it is a matter of considerable importance and urgency-if not urgency certainly importance. In following the reports in the prairie wheat pool newspapers, and other newspapers, one finds conflicting accounts as
868	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion to the nature and extent of the problem of moving grain to the port terminal and from there to the export market.
Some would maintain that the cause of the problem has to do with C.P.R. inefficiencies. Others say that the problem with grain movement has to do with the inadequate terminal and port facilities. Still others contend that there is really no great problem at all; that if it is a problem it is not a serious one because they maintain that grain shipments this year are actually ahead of those for the same period in the previous year.
I should like to hear from the minister some statement which would clarify this situation. Just to what extent is there a problem in the movement of grain? Second, has this problem been of such an extent that it has caused Canada to forgo any additional export sales? Certainly I did notice in the Western Producer, which is the publication of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, the statement that Canada has had to forgo additional sales because it simply was not able to meet any further contractual obligations. I hope that at this point the minister will make a statement which will help clarify the situation and dispel any doubts.

-at the beginning of the crop year, at the time the Canadian Wheat Board entered into the very large contract for delivery of wheat to the Soviet Union, I said that the government was establishing a target of exports for this crop year of approximately
DEBATES	February 7, 1966
600 million bushels of wheat and wheat flour. This was approximately 5 million bushels higher than the highest total achieved in any previous crop year, that is, which was achieved in the crop year 1963-64.
I also said at that time that the attainment of this target would require the utmost efficiency and the greatest good fortune. In fact, our exports of wheat so far this crop year, from August 1, 1965 to January 26, 1966 have been approximately 275 million bushels, and in the same period, or for a few days longer, of the crop year 1963-64 when we obtained almost the target figure that I fixed this year, exports were 274 million bushels. As you can see from this comparison, we are just about on target.
Exports of all grains-and as I recollect the hon. gentleman's question, it was relating to grain and not only to wheat-exports in the two periods were 335 million bushels this year, and 324 million bushels in 1963-64.
From the point of view of our exports of all grain we are doing somewhat better than we did in the previous record year. Under these circumstances it is not surprising that the Wheat Board has found it necessary to turn down certain prospective business that offered. I do not know how much business we might have got if our facilities had not been taken up so fully, but there were inquiries which could not be pursued.
I should like in conclusion to say, Mr. Speaker, that in fact the wheat board is doing very well in attaining the targets that we fixed early in the year.
